# Preface.

The history of the Order of the Knights Templar has recently occupied the public's attention once again. Both ancient and modern writers who have described the history of these famous knights have always been divided into two parties: one side portrays them as entirely guilty and deserving of the harsh fate that befell them, while the other side depicts them as completely innocent, sacrificed to the tyranny and greed of Philip the Fair <note>Philip IV of France (1268–1314), whose desire for the Order's wealth and power led to their sudden arrest and eventual dissolution.</note>. 

The obscurity of the era in which this Order flourished, the complete lack of evidence that could serve to justify these knights, and even the mutilated and ambiguous nature of the trial records <term>trial records: originally *proceßakten*, referring to the legal transcripts from the early 14th-century inquisitions</term> that still exist here and there, favor the opinion of those who—following Dupuy, Gürtler, and others—declare this Order to be guilty. In more recent times, Messrs. Anton and Nicolai <note>Karl Gottlob von Anton and Friedrich Nicolai were 18th-century scholars who researched the Templars' alleged secret doctrines and symbols.</note> have, in various ways, occupied themselves with the investigation of the accusations—

### Introduction.

The present history <note>A "pragmatic history" refers to a style of historical writing popular in the 18th century that focused on cause and effect and sought to draw moral or political lessons from the past.</note> concerns the fates of an order of knights <term>Ritterorden: a society of knights, typically religious and military in nature, formed during the Crusades</term>, which arose initially from charity and compassion, and was then elevated by the necessity and needs of the times. It is the history of an order that, powerful through its riches, famous for the bravery of its members, successful in its beginning, and subsequently possessing the respect of its era, was finally overthrown through slander and annihilated by the combined authority of two European powers <note>This refers to the alliance between King Philip IV of France and Pope Clement V, who orchestrated the dissolution of the Order in the early 14th century.</note>.

Its origin, its great deeds, the famous men who emerged within it, its Grand Master <term>Großmeister: the supreme head of the Order</term>, and finally the share it had in the events of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, deserve the attention of the historian and the philosopher just as much as the history of any other knighthood. # Introduction to the History and Defense.

historians of those times mention this Order, some with praise, others with censure, depending on their preconceived opinions; yet it never suffered the fate of being degraded through excessive flattery. But soon after its extermination, people felt entitled to portray it in such dark colors that the original itself finally became unrecognizable through them. What one finds about the Order in most historians is so little impartial, so far removed from all sound criticism and probability, that it seems as if these knights appeared on the world stage for one hundred and eighty-four years only to become an eternal stumbling block <note>The author uses the phrase "Stein des Anstoßes," a biblical idiom (stumbling block) referring to something that causes disagreement or difficulty.</note> for subsequent history.

### VI.

More than two hundred justifying documents have been added to this edition which are missing from the others—and which have provided us with superfluous material for achieving our purpose. First, one must exclude all those which contain only praise for the knights, which speak of their origin, their deeds, the donations made to them, and the privileges granted to them.

In the present work, I have applied every effort to properly organize the material without sparing anyone nor causing offense; my intention was as little to conceal the faults of the Knights Templar as it was to diminish their virtues. Even the most impartial historian cannot always resist partiality, and is often carried away at a time when he believes himself most strongly armed against it. Perhaps I myself have not remained entirely free of this reproach. The great qualities of heroes arouse our respect and admiration; their misfortune demands our compassion; one is moved and, at the same time, incensed against the authors of their misery. ### of the Order of the Knights Templar.

...men <note>Completing the word from the previous page, likely "Menschen" (men/people).</note>, whom one deems worthy of a better fate. The history of the Knights Templar is more capable than any other of arousing such feelings. Within it, one finds those rare virtues, that enterprising zeal, and that intrepidity which constitute the true heroic character, as well as that weight of fate which ignites our compassion and our indignation, and finally, examples of human weakness that demand our complete indulgence. In the midst of such subjects, it is indeed difficult to keep the spirit free and the heart indifferent.

But however differently the conduct of the Templars and their fate have affected me, I can confidently assert that I have allowed myself to be carried away neither to cowardly flattery, nor to insidious deception, nor to the glossing over of criminal acts. I sought to represent these knights as they were, and even if I did not always rail against their faults, I have nevertheless always presented them with the same frankness as their virtues.

The kings and popes who played a part in this history appear here sometimes in a good light and sometimes in a bad one, depending on whether their conduct seemed to me to deserve praise or blame. # Introduction to the History and Defense

An immeasurable number of children's skulls! It is actually a good thing when such accusations are so greatly exaggerated, for in this way they completely lose the slightest semblance of probability. This entire passage proves, strictly speaking, nothing other than the greed of **Henry VIII** and the hatred of his ministers toward the religious orders. There are slanders so greatly exaggerated, so far beyond all probability, that they finally redound to the glory of those against whom they are directed; this is because they reveal the passion of the accusers too clearly and rob them of all credibility. The incredible accusations with which the entire **Order of the Temple** <note>The Knights Templar, a Catholic military order founded in 1119 and suppressed in 1312 following accusations of heresy and immorality</note> has been branded belong to this class.

The succession of the **Grand Masters** of this Order has cost us no less effort. None of those who have provided us with such lists agreed with one another; it was therefore necessary to compare, clarify, and refute. We now leave it to the reader to decide whether our own list is more correct, or merely less deficient, than the rest. We knew that such a written list is preserved in **England** <note>f</note>, but after several futile attempts to obtain it, we had given up hope. This misunderstanding has generated several other errors of this kind, as we shall see in the following.

# History of the Knights Templar.

### History of the Knights Templar. ###

But in the eleventh century, these journeys were undertaken most frequently; they were made, as it were, into a religious law, and it seemed as if no one were a Christian who had not been to Jerusalem at least once h). The hardships and dangers of the long journey, the ill-treatment one had to endure from the infidels <note>original: *Ungläubigen*; in this context, the author refers to the Seljuk Turks and other Muslim groups who controlled the routes at the time.</note> along the way—everything was courageously overcome. Thousands of pilgrims, of both sexes and all nations, arrived before the gates of Jerusalem, where they either had to pay a gold coin for entry or remain outside the city walls, exposed to the harassment of the infidels and a total lack of all necessities. These difficulties were partially resolved in the year 1099, when Jerusalem was conquered for the first time by the Crusaders. However, the natives of the land were now incensed against the Christians; they gathered together, occupied the heights, and lay in ambush along the road to more securely fall upon the foreign travelers, whom they regarded as sworn enemies of Muhammad <note>original: *Mahomed*</note> and his religion.

To avenge these insults and put an end to the robberies, several knights—fired by compassion and the resolution of a pure life—conceived the idea of dedicating themselves to the protection of pilgrims, the securing of the roads, and the guard—

### Hugo von Payens.

Neither ambition nor a desire for expansion were part of their plan at the very beginning. As long as the **Order** was not yet [officially] approved, they did not think of increasing their numbers; instead, they lived quietly and simply, while supporting travelers with money they had collectively pooled or received through the generosity of princes. Brotherly love and the support of the needy fueled their zeal; always vigilant and concerned about the dangers to which the **pilgrims** might be exposed, they were tireless day and night in escorting them, waiting for them at the **seaports** and not leaving them until they knew they were in safety.

Thus the first seven to eight years passed amidst constant labor and danger, through which they earned the respect of all **Eastern Christians**. These soon realized what advantages the Eastern Church could receive from them if they could be persuaded to increase their numbers. **King Baldwin** first suggested this thought to them and provided them with the means for its execution. ### Hugh of Payens.

They rejoiced to be the first to promote such a praiseworthy institution and turned to **Count Thierry of Alsace**, who favored this donation so much that the houses **Godfrey** owned were very soon transformed into churches and monasteries; in this, several other nobles of **Flanders** followed their example b).

Since the Rule of **Saint Augustine**, which they had adopted on the day of their union, was not found entirely suitable to instruct them regarding the means by which they should combine the craft of war with religious duties, the Council decided that they should receive their own written Rule, which, for the sake of greater validity, was to be confirmed by the **Pope** and the **Patriarch of Jerusalem**. 

A multitude of historians assert, and it remains a tradition in the **Cistercian Order** to this day, that **Saint Bernard** was commissioned to draft this Rule; however, one rightly doubts whether he actually undertook the task. Namely, the Rule found under his name in the acts of the councils and elsewhere (c) can only be a mere extract of the former, to which some regulations for the **General Chapters** <term>General Chapter: A formal assembly of the leaders and representatives of a religious order to manage its affairs and discipline.</term> were added. In this Rule, one finds neither the writing style nor the emphasis and fire observed in **Bernard’s** other writings; indeed, one even encounters barbaric expressions <note>The author uses "barbaric" in a linguistic sense, referring to "Low Latin" or non-classical vocabulary common in the Middle Ages but beneath the standards of a scholar like Bernard.</note> that do not correspond at all to the usual purity of his style (d).

...had to be considered an independent chapel for them. The **Priory** or **Preceptory** <term>Preceptory (Präceptoratshäuser): A manor or estate under the control of a Preceptor, serving as a local headquarters for the Templars</term> houses, on the other hand, were more substantial and housed a larger number of knights, squires, and chaplains. The spiritual brothers were under the authority of an elder clergyman, who sometimes held the title of **Prior**, but the entire clergy of the house was subordinate to a knight, who was called a **Preceptor** or **Master**. This man presided over the **chapters** <term>Chapter (Kapiteln): The formal governing assembly of the members of a religious or military order</term>, oversaw the general order, dictated punishments for minor or major offenses, and referred the members to the priests for **absolution** <note>The formal forgiveness of sins granted by a priest</note>.

The chaplains were responsible for the parishes of the Order and were not bound by a **proof of nobility** <term>Proof of Nobility (Adelsprobe): The requirement to demonstrate aristocratic lineage to qualify for high-ranking positions</term>; instead, they received their authority directly from the **Pope** <margin>w) Volume 2 of the *Great Councils of Britain* <note>original: "T. The members of the Order who were sent into the provinces by the Pope were, like the superiors, entitled to accept **postulants** <note>Candidates seeking to join the Order</note>, on the condition that they present them to their superiors to be questioned regarding the motivations for their decision. They had recognized the flaws in those suits of all-iron armor with which knights covered themselves, and through which they became indeed invulnerable, but not invincible. ...provides teachings and regulations <gloss>u)</gloss>. This writing dates, at the latest, from the year 1135; and since Bernard mentions nothing at all in it regarding the Rule <term>Rule</term> <note>The "Latin Rule," a code of 72 clauses governing the behavior and spiritual life of the Templars, approved at the Council of Troyes.</note> which he was supposed to draft for the Order, there is some reason to doubt whether he ever drafted any Rule other than the regulations contained in this writing.

To be sure, the Knights Templar were eventually forced to relax much of this original strictness, though this was compensated for by other advantages. As soon as the Order was in a position to take troops into its pay, it became necessary to appoint many members as overseers, where it would then have been unseemly if they had been expected to repair their own equipment <note>original: "Equipage." In this context, it refers to the horses, armor, and baggage required for a knight's service.</note> themselves. The officer necessarily had to be distinguished from the soldier by something, remaining in one place less than before and ranging further afield, partly to train his men and partly to attend to the other duties of his position. Certainly, this meant placing "two swords" <note>A reference to the medieval "Doctrine of the Two Swords," implying the Order held both spiritual authority and physical, military power.</note> into their hands, and in the end, the cleric had to give way to the knight; yet this was the very spirit of the Order, the aim and intention of its founder, who thereby found the means to make himself useful and necessary to the public.

To the description that Saint Bernard provides of the Templars in the aforementioned writing, one can add that they the—

Since the Order only gradually attained that form of government which would later be observed in its structure, we wish to postpone speaking of its superiors and their specific duties until further on, as they were initially, as a rule, designated only by the ambiguous name, <term>Procurators</term> <note>The term "Procurator" usually refers to a legal agent or administrator; here, it suggests the early Templar leaders had not yet adopted the formal military titles like "Grand Master" or "Preceptor" that defined their later hierarchy.</note>. One source claims it happened under Gelasius II in the year 1119, and cites as proof a passage from Matthew Paris that is no longer to be found <gloss>w)</gloss>, and which contradicts the opinion of that English historian himself, who explicitly states—following William of Tyre—that the Templars persisted for a long time in their laudable principles <gloss>x)</gloss>.

News arrived that the inhabitants of the East <note>German: 'Morgenländer'. The most important business that Eberhard conducted in France concerned **Humbert of Beaujeu**, the third of that name.

This powerful and wealthy lord had spent some years of his youth in the most unrestricted enjoyment of life, after which he began to feel remorse and vowed to go to the Levant for a time to atone for his sins by fighting against the infidels. The latter was very concerned with keeping Humbert in the neighborhood of his monastery, because the monastery and the ecclesiastical estates found in him a powerful protector.

—they believed they now saw the favorable moment to regain their former possessions; and since they were accused of cowardice by their soldiers, they hastily assembled a considerable army and marched to the banks of the Jordan, where they camped on the Mount of Olives to rest, intending then to take the city by surprise all at once.

At their sudden appearance, everyone was gripped by fear and terror, all the more so because the city found itself without a garrison and almost without defense. The Knights of the Temple and of the Hospital <note>The Hospitallers, or Order of Saint John.</note>, who were still in the city and had already saved it once before during the King's absence, immediately took up arms along with the citizenry. ## Fifth Grand Master.
## Bertrand von Blanquefort.
### Year 1154 bis 1168.

<margin>1154</margin>The beginning of this Grand Mastership is remarkable due to the disputes that arose between the Eastern <note>Referring to the Latin clergy in the Crusader States of the Levant, known as "Outremer."</note> bishops and the Hospitallers <note>The Knights Hospitaller, or the Order of St. John. Although this is a history of the Templars, both military orders often shared the same legal struggles regarding church authority.</note> regarding the privileges that the latter had received from the Holy See. The clergy could not look on calmly while the knights were directly dependent only on the Pope, paid no tithes <term>Tithes: a tenth of one's annual produce or earnings, formerly taken as a tax for the support of the church and clergy.</term>, were exempt from the general ban <note>Excommunication or interdict.</note>, and could either appoint or grant the benefices <term>Benefice: a church office that provides an income, usually from land or tithes, to the person holding it.</term> of their clergy at their own discretion. The matter was eventually brought to Rome, and the Patriarch <note>Fulcher of Angoulême, the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem.</note>, who was counting on the favor of Anastasius’s successor <note>Pope Adrian IV, the only Englishman to ever hold the papacy.</note>, set out on the journey himself along with seven other bishops, despite being nearly a hundred years old. It is not known what the Hospitallers answered to these complaints, but it is known that their deputies arrived before the Patriarch and won the Pope over to their side. The Patriarch also noticed this by the frosty reception he encountered. Both parties eventually received an audience, and the matter was investigated for some time without a judgment being issued. Dhafer <note>Al-Zafir (1133–1154), the youngest Fatimid Caliph to take the throne at that time.</note>, the twelfth Fatimid <note>The Fatimid Caliphate was a Shia Islamic dynasty that ruled much of North Africa and the Levant from the 10th to the 12th century.</note> Caliph, a young man entirely devoted to a life of luxury, had conceived such a violent passion for Nazer—or Nosereddin—the son of the Vizier <note>A high-ranking political advisor or minister.</note> Al-Abbas, that he could live neither day nor night without him. Al-Abbas, who was jealous of his son’s honor and dissatisfied with the Caliph, invited him, along with two of his favorites, to a banquet intended to last late into the night. The Vizier and his son then used this opportunity to murder all three and threw their bodies into a well. The following day, Al-Abbas went to the palace and inquired after the Caliph; when he did not appear, Al-Abbas had all of the Caliph's courtiers murdered, as if they were to blame for his disappearance. **Blanquefort** <note>Bertrand de Blanquefort, who served as the sixth Grand Master of the Knights Templar from 1156 to 1169</note> stood at the head of his Order for nearly ten more years thereafter. From all that we have cited since the year 1153, it is clear that it was indeed **Blanquefort** who was captured by **Nur ad-Din** <note>The Sultan of Aleppo and Damascus, a major adversary of the Crusaders</note>, and not **Tramelay** <note>Bernard de Tremelay, the fourth Grand Master, who died at the Siege of Ascalon in 1153</note>, who, according to **du Cange** <note>Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange (1610–1688), a highly influential French scholar of the Middle Ages</note>, was supposedly captured by **Saladin** *w)*.

In this year, **Pope Hadrian** <note>Adrian IV, the only English-born Pope in history</note> saw himself forced, due to the frequent abuses of the privileges granted to the clergy, to revoke most of them. On the other hand, those of the **Templars** were not only exempted from this, but were once again expressly confirmed by this Pope, so necessary were they considered in the current state of affairs *x)*.

From the year 1150 to 1158, the **Templars** expanded their holdings in **Sicily**, **Spain**, **France**, **England**, and **Germany**, partly through donations and partly through purchase; to list all of these individually here would be too extensive, therefore we will only indicate below the writings in which they may be read *y)*.

## History of the Templars. Book Two.

<margin>1161</margin> In the year 1161, the captivity of the Prince of Antioch <note>Raynald of Châtillon, who had been captured by the forces of Aleppo in 1160 and would remain in prison for fifteen years</note> caused some unrest in his states; therefore, Baldwin <note>Baldwin III, King of Jerusalem (reigned 1143–1163)</note> hurried there and stayed for some time to restore several important strongholds. Toward the end of the campaign, according to his custom, he wished to use some laxatives <note>Purging the body through "evacuative" medicines was a standard medical practice in the Middle Ages</note> and entrusted himself to a foreign physician who, it is said, administered a slow-acting poison to him. He died at the beginning of the year 1162, in the thirty-third year of his age, after a twenty-year reign, and was mourned even by the <term>Saracens|A term used by medieval Europeans to describe Muslim populations, particularly those in the Holy Land</term>. It was suggested to Nur ad-Din <note>The Sultan of Aleppo and Damascus, and a formidable opponent of the Crusaders</note> that he should take advantage of the subjects' consternation and invade Palestine while they were occupied with Baldwin's funeral, but his answer was worthy of his noble soul: "He did not wish," he said, "to take advantage of another’s misfortune, and such a hero as Baldwin well deserved that his subjects be granted time to mourn his loss." He was one of the greatest princes of the <term>Orient|The "Morgenland" or East, specifically referring here to the Crusader States and their neighbors</term>, and alongside Nur ad-Din, the only one in all of Asia who deserved to rule over others. Since Baldwin left no children, the throne then passed to his brother Amalric or Amauri.

<margin>1162</margin> Amalric entered upon his reign in his twenty-seventh year but stood far below his predecessor in terms of character. ### 134

[Shawar was] now master of Cairo, but met Shirkuh <note>Asad ad-Din Shirkuh bin Shadhi, a Kurdish general and uncle of Saladin</note> with ingratitude, sent him back unkindly, and even refused to pay what he had promised Nur ad-Din <note>Nur ad-Din Zengi, the Sultan of Aleppo and Damascus</note>. This wing pretended as if it wanted to flee; however, while the Christians pursued them with great heat, the remaining Muslims fell upon the Christians and carried out a great massacre i). Almost all of the Templar soldiers and the <term>Turcopoles|Light cavalry units, often consisting of locally recruited soldiers, who fought alongside the Crusader orders</term> remained on the field, and out of sixty knights, only seven escaped with their lives. Both sides fought like desperate men; ten thousand of the Christians remained on the field, and the number of prisoners was even greater. Raymond, Bohemond, Joscelin, and Hugh of Lusignan were taken as captives to Aleppo, while Nur ad-Din pursued his victory, returned immediately, and captured the castle of Harem. These two events, which William of Tyre <note>original: "Wilhelm von Tyrus," the primary historian of the early Kingdom of Jerusalem</note> places in the years 1165 and 1167, actually belong to the second year of Amalric's reign, and consequently to the year 1164. It has been claimed, entirely without foundation, that Blanchefort <note>Bertrand de Blanchefort, the Grand Master of the Templars</note> was present at this defeat.

<margin>1167</margin>
Toward the middle of September 1167, the Archbishop of Caesarea and Odo de St. Amand <note>who would later become Grand Master of the Temple</note>, arrived from Constantinople at the port of Tyre. They were accompanied by the daughter of Emperor Manuel <note>Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos</note>, who was intended to be the bride for Amalric <note>King Amalric I of Jerusalem</note>. Through this close connection with the Greek Emperor, Amalric’s ambition was reawakened, and he once again formed the resolution to turn his weapons against Egypt. To that end, he sent William of Tyre <note>the famous medieval historian and prelate</note> to Constantinople to draw the Emperor into his interests, while he also sought to investigate the leanings of the two Grand Masters <note>the heads of the Templars and the Hospitallers</note>. 

<margin>1168</margin>
The Grand Master of the Hospitallers blindly approved of the King’s entire plan. Enticed by the promise that the first city conquered should belong to him, he gathered his troops and took to the field, without further considering that by doing so, a peace he himself had solemnly sworn was being broken.

## Bertrand de Blanquefort.

The situation with the Knights Templar was quite different, for they absolutely refused to yield to the King in this matter. Blanquefort <note>Bertrand de Blanquefort, the Grand Master of the Templars</note> represented to him that they had not taken up arms to make such poor use of them; that it would be contrary to all fairness and justice to now invade Egypt while its inhabitants were relying on the faith and integrity of the Christians; and that the peace must be held sacred, as the Procurator General <note>a high-ranking officer in the Order</note> of his Order had solemnly sworn to it. # Philip of Nablus.
<meta>signature mark: K</meta>

...find Philip of Nablus listed as Grand Master. It would be strange if history spoke of Philip and his Grand Mastership—which lasted only a few months—and had entirely forgotten Andreas, who must have ruled for at least five years (that is, from 1155 to 1160).

Philip was from the Milly family in Picardy <note>A region in northern France</note>, and later became the lord of Nablus in Syria. Before his change of status <note>meaning his transition from secular life to a religious military order</note>, he was married and had two daughters. After the death of his wife, he entered the Order of the Temple and rose to its highest dignity, though he resigned from this position before Easter 1171 *z)*. In September 1169, alongside the Grand Master of the <term>Hospitallers</term> <note>The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem</note>, he signed a donation made by Amalric <note>Amalric I, King of Jerusalem</note> in his capacity as Grand Master of the Temple *a)*. In October of that year, he was at Ascalon, where Amalric had gathered his troops to invade Egypt once again.

The King advanced toward Damietta <note>A strategic port city in Egypt</note> and, through carelessness, set up camp exactly in the area where the city was most strongly fortified. The siege lasted fifty days, during which time the defenders burned his fleet, and his army was decimated by hunger and disease. Thus, after a truce was concluded, Amalric found himself forced to return once more without having accomplished his goal...

### Seventh Grand Master.
## Odo of St. Amand.

Philip was succeeded by Odo of St. Amand, a French nobleman who had initially served among the secular troops but later transferred to the Knights Templar, distinguishing himself above others through many great qualities. His piety went so far that he even persuaded his wife to take the veil in the Benedictine convent at Clermont and renounce the world 1). He was handsome, tall, and pleasant in his conduct. Through these and other merits, he rose to the rank of Grand Master and became acquainted with King Amalric, who first appointed him Imperial Marshal, then High Cupbearer <term>High Cupbearer</term> <note>A high-ranking honorary position in the royal court; though it sounds domestic, it was a significant political office</note>, and made use of him in many important matters.

While Amalric stayed with the Emperor in Constantinople, one festival and festivity followed another in quick succession, as it were; in the intervals, they discussed the condition of Palestine and the means to keep the infidels <note>original: "Ungläubigen"; a term used by the author to refer to the Muslim forces</note> in check. As soon as a treaty was finalized between the two rulers, Amalric hurried back home.

There, he had the frustration of learning that during his absence, Nur ad-Din <note>The Zengid Sultan of Syria</note> had seized three locations and devastated the region of Tripoli; furthermore, that the Archbishop of Tyre, who had traveled to Europe two years earlier to seek support, had returned empty-handed; finally, that an apostate knight, at the head of a troop he had obtained from the Saracens, was laying waste to Cilicia <note>A region in south-coastal Asia Minor</note> with the intention of forcing his way to the throne of Armenia. He laid claim to this throne following the death of the late Prince Thoros, whose brother he was. This Thoros had been one of the most powerful patrons of the Knights Templar, and his brother, the apostate Melik or Melier <note>Historically known as Mleh of Armenia</note>, had himself been a Knight Templar. It is not known whether he was expelled from the Order or fled on his own to assert his claims; however, it is certain that he deposed his nephew Thomas from the throne and was the first Christian knight to form an alliance with the infidels to secure an inheritance that he had renounced by virtue of his religious vows. Furthermore, future disputes were to be decided by a committee of knights from both sides by a majority of votes. Should they be unable to reach an agreement, their mutual friends were to deliver the judgment; and if even this were insufficient, the matter was to be brought before the Grand Masters for a final decision.

This treaty was sent to the Pope and confirmed by him *k)*. Some date it to the year 1182, but this is incorrect, as both Odo and Alexander <note>Pope Alexander III (c. 1100–1181), who presided over the Third Council of the Lateran and supported the military orders.</note> had already died before then.

In this year, 1179, the clergy renewed their habitual complaints against the privileges of the two Orders <note>The Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller.</note>, and for this reason, Alexander <note>Pope Alexander III, who reigned from 1159 to 1181.</note> held the Third Lateran Council. At this assembly, all clergy were forbidden from associating with excommunicated persons, or from accepting tithes <term>tithes; a tenth part of agricultural produce or income paid as a tax to the church</term>, churches, and the like from laypeople without the consent of their bishops, and so forth.

The knights remained undisturbed in the possession of their privileges. Regarding the churches which they themselves had founded and which were served by their own chaplains, the Council permitted them to appoint or remove their priests without the intervention of the bishops.

[concluded] treaties, as is evident *l)*. In a Spanish chronicle, a certain Brother Herminda is named as Grand Master of this year, who is said to have had some disputes with Ferdinand Escasa, Grand Master of Calatrava <note>A Spanish military order founded in 1158 to defend the fortress of Calatrava from the Moors.</note>, but he was probably merely a Preceptor <term>Preceptor; a high-ranking regional administrator or officer within a military order</term> or deputy Grand Master of the Order in Spain. The same applies to Hugh Godfrey—or Gaufried of Cognac—whom the historians of Provence and Languedoc *m)* name as Grand Master in the year 1176. This Gaufried was from the house of the Counts of Marseille and a favorite of Alfonso, King of Aragon, whom he accompanied in his undertaking against the city of Nice, and for whom he brought about the peace between him and the Count of Toulouse. However, he was never Grand Master of the Order, much less Arnold’s successor in the year 1176, because at that time both were still only deputy Grand Masters. Historians were led into this error by the title *Master of the Temple* <note>original Latin: "Magister Templi"</note>, which was, however, easy to correct, as Dom Vaissette <note>Jean Joseph Vaissette (1685–1756), a Benedictine historian known for his work on the history of Languedoc.</note> himself cites a treaty from the year 1176 established between Vital, Abbot of Fontfroide, and Brother Raymond of Canet, in which the latter—notwithstanding that he was only Commander <term>Commander; the head of a small estate or local branch of a military order, known as a commandery</term> of the House of Janes (Mas de Janes)—[was called] Master.

### History of the Templars. Book Three.

Hardly had the two Grand Masters <note>The Grand Master of the Templars, Arnold of Torroja, and the Grand Master of the Hospitallers, Roger de Moulins.</note> signed the latest truce with Saladin, when they sent several knights to the Pope to inform him of it and to represent to him that they would long be unable to resist the enemy unless they received support. Alexander III immediately issued two letters, one to all Christian monarchs <note>original: "Potentaten"</note>, the other to all prelates, in which he described the sorrowful state of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and promised those who would undertake the expedition the same indulgences <note>The remission of temporal punishment for sins, a primary motivation for crusaders.</note> that his predecessors had granted. The same knights who were sent to Rome were also the bearers of these letters; they traveled from Rome to Normandy, where they presented the letters to the kings of France and England, who were holding a conference at Chinon on April 27, 1181.

<margin>1181</margin> Both rulers were deeply moved by the tragic state of affairs in the East and promised immediate support t). # History of the Templars. Book Four.

Standing like a lioness whose young have been stolen, the Templar knight, after his last comrade had been struck to the ground, defended himself alone against all, striking down everything around him that came too near. Even the Muslims <note>original: "Muselmänner"</note> paused in astonishment, hardly trusting their own eyes. Deaf to all else, he continued to defend himself until at last, pierced by a multitude of lances and arrows, he fell to the earth and breathed out his heroic spirit.

Because he had been seated upon a white horse and wore shining armor, the Muslims, upon seeing him fall, raised a loud cry of joy, believing they had slain Saint George of the Christians. The rumor was widespread at that time, and had even reached the Muslims, that Saint George had often been seen fighting at the head of the Crusader troops <note>original: "Kreuztruppen"</note> upon a white horse. Soon, the knight's body was surrounded by a crowd of curious onlookers, some of whom fought over the smallest piece of his armor, while others smeared their faces and heads with the earth stained by his blood, as if they believed they might thereby become heirs to his bravery.

King Guy or Veit <note>original: "Veit," a German variant of the name Guy or Guido.</note> of Lusignan was a weak man who could not withstand the arguments of the Grand Master, and he spent the night drawing up the march and issuing orders, which were very poorly received. The following morning the army moved out: Raymond, who was supposed to know the land best, was at the head; the King with the True Cross <note>A relic believed to be the actual cross of Jesus' crucifixion, carried by the Crusaders as a powerful holy talisman in battle.</note> was in the middle; and the Templars were in the rearguard, as it was the most dangerous post. As soon as the enemy became aware of this, he abandoned the siege of Tiberias and harassed the Christians with his light troops on their right and left during their march, with the intention of luring them into an unfavorable position. The rearguard suffered the most because the Saracen <note>A term used by medieval Europeans to describe Arab Muslims.</note> cavalry blocked all passes where fresh water or support could have been obtained. Every step had to be fought for, and after a laborious march of a day and a night, the Christians found themselves enclosed in an uneven, narrow region full of ravines, where moreover not a drop of water was to be found. Now the Sultan <note>Saladin (Salah ad-Din), the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty.</note> had achieved his aim.

The King turned to Raymond for good advice, and the latter maintained that one must remain in this poor position. It was the height of summer, and the Christians had to contend not only with fatigue, but also with thirst and the burning rays of the sun; in short, here nature itself seemed to have conspired against them. Abandoned and surrounded on all sides, the Templars succumbed to the multitude, and not a single one returned to his own people, as most remained on the field <note>original: "auf dem Platz blieben," a common idiom meaning they were killed in battle.</note>, while the rest were taken prisoner. # Terricus.

<note>Terricus, also known as Terric, was a high-ranking Templar who served as the Grand Preceptor and acting Grand Master after the disastrous defeat at Hattin.</note>

### O 2

Some modern authors have asserted that both Grand Masters remained <note>meaning they fell on the battlefield</note>, but this is false; for the Grand Master of the Hospitallers <note>The Knights of the Hospital of Saint John.</note> escaped to Ascalon, and Terricus was still living in Rome in the year 1199, as we shall see z). After this bloody encounter, Saladin commanded his generals to spread out across Palestine and to strike down all who resisted them. In this manner, in less than three months, he made himself master of more than fifteen places, including castles and fortresses, among which were Faba <note>The castle of La Fève.</note>, Sidon, Arsuf <note>original: "Assur."</note>, and several other strongholds of the Templars, which were defended only by women and old men. Acre <note>original: "Acra."</note> surrendered without a single sword-stroke, and Caesarea was taken by storm, plundered, and transformed into a heap of stones. The small band of Templars still remaining in Gaza refused to surrender, even though Saladin promised to spare their lives. They could not, they said, resolve to do so until Ascalon had fallen, which Saladin was then besieging. Gaza held out for several more weeks, and later surrendered under the same conditions as Ascalon: namely, that the King <note>Guy de Lusignan, the King of Jerusalem.</note>, the Grand Master of the Temple, and several other noble prisoners should be set at liberty within six months a).

For the departure from the city, every man was to pay ten gold thalers, every woman five, and every child two; those, however, who could not pay this were to become slaves.

After these articles were presented to and signed by the most prominent men of the city, the Knights of the Temple <note>The Templars</note> and the Hospitallers <note>The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem</note>, the keys of the city were sent without delay to Saladin. The Sultan immediately ordered the bells to be melted down, the altars torn down, the images destroyed, and all traces of Christianity obliterated. Upon the church tower of the Templars stood a great copper cross; the Christians could hardly bear to witness its tearing down, for as it tumbled to the ground, they let out a terrible cry and nearly took up arms once more. ### History of the Templars. Fourth Book.

After various skirmishes, a serious engagement took place, which continued with great intensity for two days but was not decisive for either side.

Toward the end of August, the Christians realized that the place <note>The city of Acre, which the Crusaders were attempting to recapture.</note> would never surrender as long as they had such a powerful enemy at their back, and they decided to offer him battle or break through his lines. the Teutonic Knights <note>original: "deutschen Herren," referring to the Order of the Teutonic Knights of St. Mary's Hospital in Jerusalem</note> adopted the same constitution, adding only the office of the Grand Hospital Warden <term>Grand Hospital Warden: the officer in charge of the order's charitable works and hospitals</term>, which they borrowed from the Knights Hospitaller <note>original: "Johannitern," the Order of St. John</note>, and subsequently added the office of the Grand Commander.

When the Grand Master neared his end, he usually handed over the seals and his ring to another knight, who was then regarded as his deputy. If the Grand Master died, his current deputy could either be dismissed or confirmed. In the latter case, everyone was required to obey him; he would convene the Chapter <term>Chapter: the governing council of the order's high-ranking members</term>, set the day for the election, and, with the approval of the members of the Chapter, choose the President of the Election. The latter appointed a second person, these first two a third, these three a fourth, the four a fifth, and so on until there were thirteen. Within this number, there had to be one priest, eight knights, and four other brothers from different provinces, whenever possible. The candidate who received the most votes was led before the high altar and presented to the assembly by the Deputy Grand Master, who, while handing him the seals and the ring, simultaneously impressed upon him his duties *h)*. The Grand Master, with the approval of the Chapter, confirmed or dismissed the high officials as well as the Preceptors <term>Preceptor: a regional commander or head of a provincial house of the order</term> of the provinces. Without the consent of the Chapter, he could not alienate any landed property, though he could, without—

The Grand Vicars of the Templar Order held unrestricted power within their specific departments *m)*; those of the Teutonic Order <note>The Teutonic Order was a German medieval military order modeled after the Templars, primarily active in the Baltic region</note> were in no way inferior to them in this regard, as they had the authority to depose their Grand Master, and indeed have deposed four of them. ### History of the Templars. Fourth Book.

The position of the **Grand Commander** <term>Grand Commander: the high-ranking official who managed the order's daily administration and finances</term> was not established until near the end of the thirteenth century. He served as the primary advisor or assessor to the Grand Master and was responsible for overseeing maritime affairs, provisions, and the treasury, for which he held the second key <note>Holding a second key ensured that the treasury could only be opened when both the Grand Master and the Commander were present, a common medieval security measure</note>. All brothers remaining at the headquarters, whether they were priests or laymen, were subordinate to him; he also appointed the physicians, surgeons, and managed the entirety of medical care. Because he was most familiar with the order’s business, the Grand Master frequently entrusted him with the government during his absence. In times of peace, he took precedence in rank over the Marshal, and in the absence of the Grand Master and the Under-Grand Master, he convened the Chapter <term>Chapter: the formal assembly of the members of a religious or military order</term>.

The **Marshal** held an equal rank with the Grand Commander and was in charge of military affairs. After the Grand Master, the knights were subject to him; he commanded them as their general and provided them with their military equipment, such as weapons, tents, ballistae <note>large mechanical engines used for hurling bolts or stones</note>, blankets, and especially horses and mules—though he was only permitted to purchase these without the Grand Master's permission in extraordinary cases. In times of war, he outranked the Equipment Overseer, the Treasurer, and the Hospital Overseer, and even the Grand Commander himself, who was then obligated to transport the Marshal's tents, chapel, and entire baggage train. During war, in the absence of the Grand and Under-Grand Master, he convened the Council of War and, in addition to a lieutenant, had two serving brothers and two Turcopoles <term>Turcopoles: light cavalry soldiers recruited from the local population in the Levant, often used as scouts or archers</term> to carry the standard, and as many

### ->Gerard de Ridefort<-

<note>Gerard de Ridefort was the Grand Master of the Templars from 1184 to 1189, known for his role in the events leading to the Battle of Hattin.</note>

The Marshal was permitted as many servants in his retinue as were necessary to care for the horses and mules. However, according to the **Statutes** <term>Statutes: the formal written laws and regulations governing the conduct of the members of the Order</term>, he could not order the signal for attack to be blown without the permission of the Grand Master, if the latter were present, unless a delay would prove dangerous. He was permitted to invite some of his friends to the infirmary table and keep them company, though this was not to happen frequently. Without permission, he could not lend horses to anyone outside the Order for more than one or two days. Since the **Marshal** and the **Preceptor** <note>also referred to here as the Grand Commander</note> often had to stand in for one another, both were strictly commanded to ensure that the absence of one or the other would go unnoticed by the ranks.

The **Hospital Overseer** was responsible for the care of the sick and the administration of the Hospitalers <term>Hospitalers: in this context, the brothers specifically assigned to medical and charitable duties within the infirmary</term>, as well as the supervision of the hospital servants and nurses. He provided them with the regulations on how the income should be used for the benefit of the sick; if these funds were exhausted, the Grand Commander was required to provide counsel and resources. However, if any funds remained, they were returned to the common treasury.

The **Equipment Overseer** <note>Historically known in the Order as the *Draper*</note> looked after the clothing and provided the knights with not only their daily attire but also their military dress, such as sword-belts, **shoulder cords**, surcoats, and so forth *q)*.

### History of the Templars. Fourth Book.

At the end of the winter, the winter clothing was handed over to the **Grand Commander** and the **Marshal** by the **Equipment Overseer**, who subsequently distributed them to those who wished to serve for free <note>likely referring to secular knights or volunteers serving for a fixed term rather than permanent members</note>. However, the Equipment Overseer was permitted to distribute the plain and worn-out clothes to the poor on his own authority. He also provided the **travel allowance** <term>travel allowance: originally "Zehrpfennig," a small sum of money given to brothers for food and lodging while traveling between houses</term> to those brothers traveling from one house to another. Without his permission, no one was allowed to keep a piece of cloth that had been gifted to him; if the cloth was sufficient to make two cloaks, the Overseer was entitled to claim half of it r).

The fifth and last high official was the **Treasurer** or **Seneschal** <term>Seneschal: a high-ranking officer who managed the domestic and financial affairs of the Order</term>, whose duty was to purchase supplies at the proper time and to ensure that food was distributed correctly without regard for a person's status. Everything that entered the treasury passed through his hands, and he also held the third key to the treasure chest <note>The treasury was typically secured with three different keys held by three different officials to ensure collective oversight</note>. If the Grand Master, while absent, required money, he would command the Treasurer to take out a loan and arrange for its repayment. In all matters not pertaining to warfare, he was required to follow the instructions of the Grand Commander. All gifts of fruit and provisions were handed over to the Treasurer,

### History of the Templars. Fourth Book.

The **Turcopolier** <term>Turcopolier: an officer in charge of the light cavalry, or Turcopoles, who were often recruited from local eastern populations</term> held supreme command over the light cavalry, and within the **Teutonic Order**, the Marshal appointed him if he found it necessary to fill this position.

The **Chapel Warden** was a knight to whom the oversight of the chapel and the church vestments <note>original: "Kirchenornat"</note> was entrusted. As long as the army was in the field and living under tents, he ensured the signal was given for divine service at the proper hour. Usually, the field chaplain held the service at a specific time, with the exception of **Nones** and **Vespers** <note>Two of the traditional "canonical hours" or prayer times; Nones occurred in the mid-afternoon and Vespers at sunset</note>, which were only held once the Marshal believed everyone had assembled. While on the march, no one was permitted to take up quarters until the chapel had been erected and the Grand Master and the Marshal were settled. In the camp, the tents were pitched in a circle around the chapel so that everyone could hear and see the divine service *u)*.

No clergyman or layman was permitted to confess to anyone other than a chaplain of the Order without special permission. The unforgivable crimes were the following three: **pederasty** <note>In the medieval monastic context, this referred generally to homosexual acts, which were strictly forbidden</note>, **apostasy** <note>The abandonment of one's religious faith or the desertion of the Order</note>—even if they had not concurrently renounced their faith—and the dishonor of shameful flight before the enemy out of mere fear. For these three cases, there was neither forgiveness nor penance; the perpetrator was ignominiously expelled from the Order, without hope of ever being readmitted.

Although these statutes, provided here in extract, are not all of the same age, some among them clearly date from the twelfth century. Consequently, they were written earlier than when the German Knights <note>The Teutonic Order</note> expanded into Germany, because one still encounters the terms <term>Besant</term> <note>A gold coin originally minted in the Byzantine Empire, commonly used by Crusaders in the Levant</note> and <term>Turcopoles</term> <note>Light cavalry units often recruited from local Middle Eastern populations</note> in them, which were not yet in use in Prussia in the thirteenth century. ### History of the Templars. Book Five.

Paez <note>Gualdim Pais, the Master of the Templars in Portugal</note>, who had established this place ten years earlier and commanded there, defended himself and his Templars so bravely that the Saracens <note>The Almohad forces from North Africa</note> were forced to retreat toward Santarém. Fortunately for King Sancho <note>Sancho I of Portugal</note>, who had shut himself inside, the English fleet was driven back to the mouth of the Tagus <note>original: "Tajo"</note> by a gust of wind. Robert <note>Robert de Sablé, the future Grand Master mentioned on the previous page</note> went ashore with five hundred men, threw himself into the stronghold, and forced the Saracens to lift the siege *i)*.

The two kings <note>Richard the Lionheart of England and Philip II Augustus of France</note> finally arrived at Messina <note>A port city in Sicily</note>, where they were forced to spend the winter, but they did not remain in agreement for long. Their ways of thinking and temperaments were too different for them to remain friends. Richard first clashed with the French and then with the citizens of Messina, whom he even besieged, leaving their city to be plundered.

This nearly caused the new crusade to fail, had the knights and nobles of both nations not persuaded both parties back to a peaceful settlement. Richard agreed that Messina should remain under the protection of the Templars and Hospitallers <note>The Order of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem</note> until he had reached an agreement with the King of Sicily. Tancred <note>Tancred of Lecce, the King of Sicily</note> proved willing to negotiate, and Philip, King of France, likewise reconciled with Richard. The alliance they had established when they first took the cross <note>A phrase meaning to join a crusade</note> was renewed.

### History of the Knights Templar. Book Five.

However, since the defenders were still strongly entrenched and determined to be buried under the ruins of the city rather than surrender without capitulation, it was signaled to them that they would be heard. On the appointed day, both kings <note>Richard I of England and Philip II of France</note>, along with the most prominent commanders of the army, gathered in the main tent of the Templars and came to an agreement with the besieged that they could depart freely with their belongings, wives, and children, on the condition:

These terms of surrender were signed by both sides; the Christians took possession of the city on the 12th of July, and the lives of the defeated served as a guarantee for the fulfillment of the conditions.

The proud King Richard <note>King Richard I of England, famously known as "the Lionheart."</note> wished to claim the greatest share of the honor for this victory and ordered his banner to be planted upon the highest towers of the city. Among others, he caught sight of the banner of Duke Leopold of Austria <note>Leopold V, who would later famously capture and imprison Richard during his journey back to England.</note> on a tower that the Duke had captured. Out of an arrogance that would later cost him dearly, Richard ordered it to be torn down, trampled, and thrown into the ditch. This insult was directed at the entire German nation, which demanded satisfaction with arms in hand. The Templars <note>The Knights Templar often acted as mediators and diplomats between the various factions of the Crusader armies.</note> intervened to mediate and thereby prevented a bloodbath, which would have brought eternal shame upon the Christians. v)

According to the old, still-existing plan of Acre, the Templars held three significant areas within the city: one was situated on the seaside; the second was the residence of the knights, called the Castle of the Temple; and the third was the Ox Market. # Robert de Sablé or Sabloil.

This capitulation <note>The formal agreement for surrender.</note> was signed by both sides; the Christians took possession of the city on the 12th of July, and the lives of the conquered served as a guarantee for the fulfillment of the conditions.

Proud King Richard <note>Richard the Lionheart of England.</note> wished to claim the largest share of the honor for this victory and ordered his banner to be placed upon the highest towers of the city. Among others, he caught sight of the banner belonging to Duke Leopold of Austria on a tower that the Duke had captured. Out of an arrogance that would later cost him dearly <note>Leopold later captured Richard during his return journey from the Crusade as revenge for this insult.</note>, Richard ordered it to be torn down, trampled underfoot, and thrown into the ditch. This insult was directed at the entire German nation, which demanded satisfaction with arms in hand. The Templars intervened as mediators and thereby prevented a bloodbath that would have been an eternal shame to the Christians v).

According to the old, still-existing plan of Acre, the Templars occupied three significant areas within it: one was located on the seaside, another was the residence of the knights—called the Castle of the Temple—and the third was the Ox Market. The King of France <note>Philip II Augustus.</note> resided in the city castle, and the King of England in the Temple Court <note>The headquarters or precinct of the Templars.</note>. Now Richard made a turn as if he intended to advance upon Jerusalem, but he saw that many in the army, especially the French, did not follow him. ### History of the Templars. Fifth Book. ###

Saladin, who on the one hand feared him and, after so much bloodshed, wished to grant his subjects some peace, replied that he was still of the same mind, and the negotiations began anew.

A three-year truce by sea and land was concluded, with the condition that Ascalon—the restoration of which had cost the Templars so much—be entirely razed <note>The destruction of Ascalon's fortifications was a significant concession, as the Crusaders had spent enormous sums rebuilding them only months prior</note>; that seven cities, among others Jaffa, Caesarea, Haifa <note>original: "Caiphas"</note>, Arsur <note>original: "Assur"</note>, and Acre along with their territories, be left to the Christians; that Lydda <note>original: "Lidda"</note> and Ramla be divided between both powers; that all cities not mentioned in the treaty, but primarily Jerusalem, should remain with the Sultan, and that in this case they <note>meaning Christian pilgrims</note> should be exempted from all customs and tribute. This was the extent of everything that the three-hundred-thousand-man-strong Christian army was able to obtain *a)*.

<margin>1193</margin>
In the following year, death freed the knights from their most formidable enemy: Saladin died. He had been the son of a governor of Tekrit <note>A historic city in modern-day Iraq</note> and had elevated himself to the <term>Caliphate</term> <note>The office of the supreme political and religious leader of the Islamic state</note> through ingratitude toward his benefactors, cunning, and treachery. He knew how to maintain himself on the throne of the Sultans through force; yet, on the other hand, he glorified his life through rare examples of self-control, moderation, and magnanimity. These qualities deserve to be known by posterity more than the legend of the "death shroud," which he supposedly had carried on a lance through Damascus to signal that death spares no man.

<margin>1194</margin>
Meanwhile, in the West, the <term>Miramolin</term> <note>A European corruption of the Arabic title "Amir al-Mu'minin," meaning Commander of the Faithful; here referring to the Almohad Caliph Yaqub al-Mansur</note> of Africa caused much trouble for the Spanish. In the year 1194, he achieved a complete victory over them at Alarcos, where the King of Castile and the military orders were utterly defeated. It is unknown what specific part the Templars played in this, as history does not sufficiently distinguish them from the other Spanish knights. It is only known that Lopez Fernand, the Grand Preceptor of Portugal, remained before Ciudad Rodrigo during this war *f)*.

### Twelfth Grand Master.
## Gilbert Horal.

Horal's reign lasted no longer than about five years. Around the time of his elevation to the Grand Mastership, the German leaders <note>This refers to the leaders of the German Crusade of 1197, launched by Emperor Henry VI</note>—uncertain about further undertakings and firmly resolved to avenge the slaughter of the inhabitants and the garrison of Jaffa—sent a delegation to the most prominent military orders. As for their **greed**, one should consider that for them, just as for any other society that possesses large estates, every new expansion of their holdings necessarily gave rise to new disputes, lawsuits, and so forth. The more they received as gifts, the more their business, difficulties, and the envy of their opponents grew, so that they could never finish with their complaints and justifications before the Roman See <note>the papal court and central administration of the Catholic Church</note>.

Under the reign of **Celestine III** <note>Pope from 1191 to 1198</note>, they entered into a dispute with the monks of **Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian**, at **Tin** <note>likely Tinj in modern-day Croatia</note> on the Dalmatian border. V. The clergy were forbidden from infringing upon the privileges of the Order or from making it difficult for its chaplains to hold divine service under any pretext.

Between two such powerful, brave knightly orders—each so jealous of its own rights—some envy was bound to arise occasionally. However, anyone who attributes all this to mere greed, and follows **Matthew Paris** <note>A famous 13th-century English monk and chronicler known for his detailed, if often biased, accounts of contemporary events</note> in assuming the cause was that the Hospitallers possessed nineteen thousand estates and lordships, while the Templars held only nine thousand, knows very little of the spirit of military and religious orders. Whenever a dispute arises between spiritual and military orders, the root cause is usually not wealth, but rather antiquity, precedence, and the services rendered to the state or the Church. In Aragon <note>A kingdom in the northeast of the Iberian Peninsula</note>, not only their persons but also their property and freedoms were included in the treaty which King Peter <note>Peter II of Aragon</note> established with the clergy and nobility of his land *n)*.

The Knights Templar in England were confirmed by the Pope in the right of sanctuary <term>sanctuary: the historical legal right for a fugitive or criminal to seek safety from arrest within the walls of a church or religious house</term>, which they had possessed until then. The knights had complained that those who fled to their houses were often taken away by force, robbed of their assets, and forced to ransom themselves. In response, Innocent <note>Pope Innocent III</note> earnestly recommended to the English prelates the abolition of this abuse. He instructed them to impose the ban <note>ecclesiastical excommunication</note> upon those who laid their hands on the unfortunate souls who were forced to seek a sanctuary in the houses of the Order *o)*. The English knights possessed this right without interruption until the complete dissolution of the Order, and their successors <note>The Knights Hospitaller, who inherited much of the Templar property</note> enjoyed it for a long time afterward.

As soon as a criminal fled into one of their houses, his name and his offense were recorded, along with whether it was an actual crime or merely fear of his—

### History of the Knights Templar. Book Five.

...creditors had moved him to seek refuge, all of which was recorded in a book. Following this, he was required to swear an oath that he would cause no damage to the house, nor give any other cause for offense, but would instead conduct himself as an upright man, promote the welfare of the house, and strictly follow the rules prescribed therein. He also swore never to leave without permission, under the penalty of losing the protection he had sought.

If he had been unfaithful to his lord, he was guarded throughout the night, unless someone provided a guarantee <note>original: Bürgschaft; a legal surety or bail</note> for his person and his conduct. If he struck anyone or incited a quarrel within the house, he was imprisoned and required to pay a fine appropriate to his offense. If he became unfaithful a second time and deceived his lord, he lost the right of sanctuary <note>original: Freystatt; a place of safety where the law could not reach a person</note> and was handed over to the secular arm <note>The civil or royal authorities, who could carry out physical punishments that the Church generally avoided</note>.

Except in the case of <term>felony</term> <note>In a medieval context, felony referred specifically to a breach of the feudal bond, such as treachery against one's lord</note> or unfaithfulness, all those who had once been received into the houses of the Order and had departed according to the regulations could be accepted a second or third time, provided they paid the customary penalty of four <term>deniers</term> <note>A common medieval silver coin</note>.

If a tenant <note>original: Pachter; a farmer or leaseholder of the Order's lands</note> or servant of these houses was convicted of having let in a woman of ill repute and having encouraged debauchery, he not only had to pay his fine but also lost the protection of the house. Also could—

# Gilbert Horal.

...no robber should receive this protection <note>The right of sanctuary or asylum within a church or religious house</note> until he had, if it were at all possible, restored what was stolen. This ancient right granted to the churches had a very laudable origin. Eutropius <note>A powerful official in the Eastern Roman Empire who ironically sought refuge in a church after trying to abolish the very same right of sanctuary</note>, who first wanted to abolish it, later deeply regretted it and a year later had to consider himself lucky to find the sanctuary <note>original: Freystatt; a place of safety where the law could not reach a person</note> that he had wanted to close to others.

We must also note that at a church council <note>original: Kirchenversammlung</note> this year, the knights of both orders <note>The Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller</note> were forbidden from accepting any church from the hand of a layman <note>A person not belonging to the clergy</note> without the permission of the bishops; this was likely because the same law, which had already been issued at the Third Lateran Council <note>A major meeting of Church leaders held in 1179 to address Church discipline and reform</note>, had been violated here and there.

Before we close the twelfth century, we wish to mention a few more benefactors of the Order. Among these are Raoul of Coucy *p)*, and the Countess of Montferrand, wife of the Dauphin <note>A title used by the lords of Auvergne, later becoming the title for the heir to the French throne</note>, Count of Clermont, who make the most honorable mention of the knights in their wills *q)*.

In the year 1195, Eleanor, Countess of Saint Quentin, granted the Order ten pounds Parisis <note>A currency based on the "Pound of Paris"</note> annually to be collected from the customs of Crépy, on the condition that a requiem mass <note>original: Todtenamt; a liturgical service for the souls of the deceased</note> be celebrated for her every year *r)*.

## Thirteenth Grand Master.
# Philip of Plessies.

<margin>1201</margin>
After a five-year term as Grand Master <term>Grand Master; the supreme head of the Order of the Temple</term>, it was not Pontius Rigaldo, as Du Cange <note>Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange (1610–1688), a highly influential French scholar of the Middle Ages</note> claims, but Philip of Plessies who took Horal’s place. History of the Templars. Book Five.

Du Plessies was from Anjou and came from a noble house already known in 1062, which is famous in the history of Brittany *w)*.

To avoid abandoning the Order's claims to Fort Gaston <note>Also known as Bagras or Gastun, a strategic fortress in the Amanus Mountains that was a point of contention between the Templars and the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia</note>, the new Grand Master, following the example of his predecessors, joined the party of Bohemond against the King of Armenia. The King, who was forced to retreat with his nephew until his troops arrived, sent a lengthy letter to the Pope, in which he first complained about the Templars and justified his conduct toward Bohemond. He then requested a favor from Innocent: that Armenia should in the future be independent of any Latin bishop, except for the Bishop of Rome or his legates, and that the Holy See alone should have the authority to impose ecclesiastical penalties <term>Ecclesiastical penalties; spiritual punishments such as excommunication or interdict used by the Church to enforce its laws</term> upon the Armenians *x)*.

# Philip of Plessies #

<margin>1202</margin>
The Pope, who was very well informed about everything, answered the King on June 1st, 1202. He did not offer any reply to the King’s complaints against the Templars, but because the King had only recently united with the Latin Church, the Pope granted his latter request so as not to completely alienate him. However, while the papal legates <term>Legates; official representatives or ambassadors of the Pope invested with his authority</term> were on their way to investigate the dispute, Leo attempted to place his nephew in possession of Antioch by force. Placing himself at the head of his troops, he forced open a city gate near the castle during the night, took possession of a portion of the city, and sought to have his nephew declared the sovereign before the legates arrived. But after three days had passed, both were forced to retreat. In this moment, the Templars forgot one of the most essential articles of their Rule of the Order; they let the banner of the Order (the *Beauseant* <term>Beauseant; the famous black and white banner of the Templars, which they were forbidden to lower or abandon in battle</term>) fly against the Armenians, hunted them out of the city, and in this manner forced them to await the arrival of the legates. To take his revenge in the meantime, Leo expelled all Templars from his states and seized the properties of the Order.

Such was the thinking of priests and laypeople alike, who were weary of atoning for the transgressions of their prince or overlord <margin>n) Ecclesiastical History, <note>original: "Histoire eccles."</note> Vol. XVI. p. 132.</margin>.

As soon as a priest of the Order of the Temple appeared under such circumstances, the people were beside themselves with joy, for he had the right to open the churches and hold divine services. <note>The Templars held special papal privileges that allowed them to open closed churches once a year and provide burials even in lands under an interdict.</note> Therefore, people crowded to join the brotherhood of a Temple house in their vicinity, if only to receive an honorable burial. The Order could also transfer this right to its secular <term>secular: here referring to lay members or associates who were not ordained monks</term> brothers who had not been personally placed under the ban <term>ban: a formal exclusion from the Church and its services</term> or excommunicated. However, because it was difficult to distinguish these individuals from others—especially in large cities or when they came from far away—the Order’s chaplains were often deceived. They sometimes granted church burials and their other rights to people who had outwitted them or whom they did not truly know. This was the first point of complaint.

# History of the Templars. Sixth Book.

Furthermore, if a bishop placed any location within his diocese <term>diocese: the district or region under the care of a bishop</term> under a ban <term>ban: also known as an interdict, a punishment where the Church stops all public religious services in a specific area</term> where the Knights Templar resided (and at that time they were to be found everywhere), the knights did not need to concern themselves with it by virtue of their privileges, and behaved as if nothing had happened. The bishops considered this a violation of church discipline; a multitude of clergy who lived from the altar <note>meaning they survived on the offerings and fees provided by parishioners for religious services</note> became impoverished because of it, and they cried out loudly when they saw how everyone hurried to the chapels of the Order. From all sides, complaints against the Order piled up in Rome, and Innocent III finally leveled bitter reproaches against the Grand Master, stating that his knights were so greatly abusing their freedoms. He exhorted him, for the sake of the Order's honor, to proceed more cautiously and to use all his authority to contest and abolish such unheard-of and offensive abuses. Finally, he commanded him to proceed with the utmost severity against all those who refused to be corrected. Innocent further complained that the clergy of the Order were having the churches opened everywhere multiple times and almost daily, and were even reading Mass with open doors and to the sound of ringing bells, whereby church discipline was degraded and the effect of the interdict was entirely nullified.

The reply from the Preceptor <term>Preceptor: a high-ranking administrator within the Templar Order</term> of France to Konrad is still extant; in it, he authorizes the proposed exchange and approves everything that might be established regarding this matter between the Bishop and Brother Bruno.

Hardly had the deputy returned when, after some preliminary arrangements, the Cistercians occupied the Abbey of Saint James, and the Templars moved into that of Saint Thomas. The official deed regarding this exchange was read and approved in a public synod <term>synod: a formal council of a church to decide on issues of doctrine or administration</term>. At that time, one often encountered knights from both orders <note>likely the Templars and the Hospitallers</note> who had been sent to the Western lands by their Grand Masters to represent the sorrowful state of Palestine to the nobility and the common people. For four years now, Rupin <note>historically known as Raymond-Roupen, a claimant to the throne of Antioch</note>, the cousin of King Leo of Armenia, had been in peaceful possession of Antioch, and the Order <note>the Knights Templar</note> lived in good harmony with the latter, until Bohemond, the Count of Tripoli, retook Antioch and the fire of discord was ignited anew. # History of the Templars. Sixth Book.

In Italy, the Bishop of Osimo made several demands against the Knights of Saint Philip of Plana, which the knights were unwilling to accept. The matter was brought before the Bishops of Fano, Jesi, and Ancona, who summoned the parties. The Bishop of Osimo demanded various ecclesiastical rights and taxes that he claimed had been withheld from him. The knights, on the other hand, asserted that he had encroached upon their lands, tithes, meadows, and pastures. The commissioners heard both parties and sent the transcript of the hearing to the Pope <note>Likely Pope Innocent III, who was the reigning pontiff in 1211 and frequently mediated disputes between the military orders and local bishops</note> for a final judgment. He decided:

1) That instead of the third that the Bishop demanded from the burial fees <note>original: "Beerdigungsgelder"; fees paid for the right to be buried in consecrated ground, a significant source of revenue for medieval religious institutions</note>, he should receive only a fourth part; and even from this, the knights were to deduct the value of the horses and armor of the deceased, which rightfully belonged to them; <note>It was standard practice for a knight's military equipment and horse to be left to his Order upon his death</note>

2) Regarding the sixth part of the income of the Church of Saint Philip, it was proven that the Bishop had previously given it away as a gift, and consequently, he could not demand it back.

3) Instead of a fourth part of the tithes of Saint Mary and Saint Marina, he was to receive only one quarter of pure grain and one quarter of mixed grain. <term>mixed grain: original "Gemangkorn," also known as maslin; a mixture of different grains, such as wheat and rye, sown and harvested together</term>

4) For the right of the pulpit <note>original: "Kanzelrecht"; a fee or legal authority associated with preaching and the administrative oversight of a parish church</note>, he was entitled to no more than two sols <note>original: "Sols"; a currency unit derived from the Roman "solidus," commonly known as a sou</note> in current coin.

5) The knights should, in the future as in the past, retain the right to appoint and... <note>The text breaks off here mid-sentence at the end of the page; the context suggests "appoint and remove" the priests of their churches</note>

Finally, the Bishop had to return the meadows and lands to the knights, though with a reservation of his right of ownership; in return, the latter [the knights] had to send back the tenants they had lured away from him and promise not to take them into their service further except with the Bishop's consent, etc. f).

A similar dispute had arisen in Italy between the knights of the **Aventine** <note>The Templars held a significant commandery on the Aventine Hill in Rome, the site of the present-day Villa del Priorato di Malta</note> and the monks of **Grottaferrata** regarding the church of **Santa Maria di Sorresco**. After investigating the claims of both sides, the Pope decided that this church, along with all its rights, should remain with the knights, and that the monks should renounce all their claims and rights to its properties, on the condition that the knights pay them thirty *sols* <term>sols: a medieval currency unit derived from the Roman solidus; in this context, it refers to a fixed annual payment</term> of feudal rent <note>original: "Lehnzinn"</note> annually in Rome on the Feast of the Assumption of Mary g).
