# History of the Templars. Sixth Book.

->### Philippe du Plessis.<-

Despite all the peaceful efforts of the Pope <note>Pope Innocent III</note> and the Eastern magnates to persuade the King of Armenia to reach a settlement with the Templars, not a single step forward had been taken. The Patriarch of Jerusalem <note>Albert of Vercelli, a key diplomat in the Crusader States</note> wished to make one final attempt and persuaded the Grand Master to send some of his knights to the King to hear his reasoning and respond to his grievances. 

But regardless of the fact that these deputies were provided with full authority to settle this long-standing quarrel, Leo <note>King Leo II of Armenia, also known as Leo the Magnificent</note> refused to engage in any negotiations. Nor would he irrevocably submit to the judgment that du Plessis <note>Grand Master Philippe du Plessis</note> had already promised to uphold. Instead, he not only seized the port of **Bonel** and several other lands from which the knights drew the majority of their food supplies, but he also stationed soldiers in their commanderies <term>commanderies: the local administrative centers and estates of a military order</term>, who lived there at the Order's expense and were instructed to prevent any goods from being removed. 

The Pope pleaded and threatened in vain; the Patriarch had to exert all his influence just to move the King toward returning the Order’s confiscated properties. Following this, the King was informed that they were willing to hear his arguments and grievances and would see that justice was done. A deadline was set, after which he was threatened with excommunication <note>the formal exclusion from the sacraments and the Christian community</note> should he persist in his current course. This threat also had no effect; the Patriarch pronounced the sentence of excommunication <note>original: "Bannsfluch"</note> against him and threatened all locals and foreigners who supported him in his acts of violence—

This step only incensed the King further. He stripped the Knights of everything they possessed in his territories, with the exception of two strongholds that resisted him. While the Knights were busy supplying their castles in the Principality of Antioch with provisions, the King destroyed all their dwellings and estates in Armenia and drove out their subjects, tenants, and vassals. One day, as the Knights—led by their Grand Master <note>Philippe du Plessis</note>—were on their way to reinforce one of their positions, the King’s men lay in wait for them in a narrow mountain pass. They fell upon the Grand Master, wounding him and several others, killed one knight, and robbed the rest of everything they owned.

Following this outrage, the Pope <note>Innocent III</note> commanded the Patriarch of Antioch, the Archbishop of Tyre, and the Bishops of Tripoli, Sidon, Nicosia, and Famagusta to publicly proclaim the ban of excommunication <term>ban of excommunication: a formal decree excluding an individual from the religious life and sacraments of the Church, a severe political and social tool in the Middle Ages</term> against the King. They were ordered to enforce this sentence in every detail until the King should have a change of heart. At the same time, the Pope wrote to the King of Jerusalem <note>John of Brienne</note>, ordering him and all his subjects to support the Templars and help them regain their rightful possessions and legal standing *h)*.

->## History of the Templars. Sixth Book.<-

The Emperor of Constantinople <note>likely Henry of Flanders</note> proved himself no less obstinate than the King of Armenia. The Pope <note>Innocent III</note> was compelled to write to him a second time, rebuking him for his injustices against the Order, from whom he withheld the fortress of Sidon <note>an ancient port city in modern-day Lebanon; the dispute here involves territories held or claimed following the Fourth Crusade</note> for no other reason than because it pleased him to do so. At the end of the letter, the Pope threatened him with the usual punishments *i)*.

This greed of the Eastern princes and this audacity in attacking Church property moved Raynaldus <note>Odoricus Raynaldus (1595–1671), a historian who continued the "Annales Ecclesiastici," a massive history of the Catholic Church</note> to say, "that it was no wonder the circumstances of the Christians in the East grew ever worse."

<margin>1212</margin>
In this year, the King of Jerusalem lost his wife <note>Maria of Montferrat, Queen of Jerusalem</note>, with whom he had fathered a daughter named Isabella <note>Isabella II, who would later become Queen of Jerusalem</note>. The Pope feared that this death might stir up new unrest and commanded the Grand Master and his knights to oppose anyone who wished to disturb the peace and harmony with an armed hand. At the same time, he recommended to them the support of King John of Brienne and the defense of his rights and states as if they were their own. To further ensure their loyalty, he commanded his legates <term>legates: high-ranking personal representatives of the Pope, sent on special missions with his full authority</term> to emphatically exhort them and, in case of necessity, even threaten them with ecclesiastical penalties <term>ecclesiastical penalties: punishments such as excommunication or interdict used by the Church to enforce discipline</term> *k)*.

As soon as Innocent <note>Pope Innocent III (reigned 1198–1216), one of the most powerful and politically active popes of the Middle Ages.</note> learned of this, he released all of King John’s subjects from their oath of loyalty and obedience, and he persuaded the King of France to declare war on him. Pandulf and his assistant arrived and brought the King to the point where he granted everything they demanded. ### William of Chartres.

Throughout the harsh winter, they continued their raids into enemy territory, but they had to endure so much from storms, disease, and famine that the army—which initially consisted of twenty thousand cavalry and one hundred thousand infantry—soon dwindled significantly. Toward the end of the campaign, a small loaf of bread was sold for twelve *deniers* or five *livres* of today’s French currency <note>The author is likely comparing the price to the French Livre of the late 18th or early 19th century to illustrate the extreme inflation caused by the famine.</note>; consequently, a great many people had to be sent away, not counting sixty-six ships filled with the poor which had already been sent back by sea in September *r)*.

On the occasion of these many unfortunate incidents, the new Grand Master, **William of Chartres**, wrote to the Pope and described to him the sorrowful condition of the Christians in the East <note>original: "Morgenland"</note>. "The Muslims <note>original: "Muselmänner"</note>," he said, "had been terrified by the arrival of the new Crusading army, so that they did not dare to show themselves; the army of **Corradin** <note>Al-Mu'azzam Isa (reigned 1218–1227), the Ayyubid Emir of Damascus, often called Corradin in Western sources.</note> was in poor condition," and so forth. On the other hand, the Christians lacked corn, barley, and all other fruits of the field because the harvest had failed, and the people of the East had hoped for provisions from the West <note>original: "Occident"</note>. However, these supplies had been delayed for so long that their distress was indescribable. Most of the knights no longer had horses, because those that had died could not be replaced; therefore, those who still wished to undertake the Crusade would have to bring everything they needed with them. Not far from Mount Carmel was a high, spacious promontory, steeply sloped on all sides, which in former times was called the "Strait," *Detroit* or *Districtum* <note>The French and Latin terms for a narrow pass or "distress" point.</note>, because of a narrow path that ran along the sea there, and upon which the Saracens used to lie in wait for the pilgrims. To deter these robbers and secure the way for the Christians, the early Templars <note>original: "alten Tempelherren"</note> had seized this high ground and kept it occupied in times of both peace and war. This year <note>1218</note>, they decided, together with the Teutonic Order <note>original: "deutschen Ritterorden," the third major military order of the Crusades</note>, to strongly fortify the site. On the accessible side, they erected two enormous, four-sided stone towers, for which such massive stones were required that two horses could scarcely pull one of them. These two towers they connected with a high, strong wall featuring embrasures <note>original: "Schiesscharten," narrow slits for firing arrows</note>, which was supported from the rear by a sloping rampart <note>original: "Wall"</note> that allowed the knights to easily ascend and descend. In the center, and at some distance from the towers, they erected a second wall parallel to the first, which ran from one end of the promontory to the other and enclosed a large space, in the middle of which a well was dug. The towers were one hundred feet <note>original: "Schuh," literally "shoes," a historical unit of measurement</note> in height and sixty-four in circumference, and their thickness was substantial enough to support two spacious vaults <note>original: "Gewölber"</note>. In older times, a fortress must have already stood here, for the foundations of two old walls were found, one of which...

This fort, which was subsequently named the **Pilgrims’ Castle** <note>original: "Pilgerschloß"; also known by its French name, Château Pelerin</note>, possessed a convenient and naturally fortified harbor. The surrounding countryside provided all necessary supplies in abundance, including timber, embankments, pastures, fruit trees, and fields for cultivation. Since the **Muslims** <note>original: "Muselmänner," a historical term used in the text for practitioners of Islam</note> held no fortified position along the coast from **Acre** <note>original: "Akkon"</note> to **Jerusalem**, the knights became masters of the entire region as far as the foot of **Mount Tabor** due to this strategic location. They compelled the inhabitants of the surrounding areas to abandon their homes. As a result, the Muslims stationed on the heights of Tabor were cut off and deprived of resources; they were eventually forced to abandon the mountain after they had razed the fortifications. The knights' goal in this undertaking was not only to fortify themselves against the enemy, but even more to establish a retreat and place of refuge from the debauchery and moral decay that was then prevalent throughout Acre <term>u</term> <note>This "u" refers to the scholarly citation in the margin.</note>.

That same year, **Theobald**, Duke of **Upper Lorraine**, granted to the Templars within his states—as a proof of his esteem—the use of his forests, the acorn mast <term>acorn mast: the fallen nuts of forest trees, which served as vital feed for livestock, especially pigs</term>, and the pastures for their cattle. In the event that their people caused any damage, he ordered that they be held to make restitution, but without penalty; and when the Preceptor <note>A high-ranking official in the Templar Order who managed a district or province</note> came to court, he, along with four men and four horses, was to be provided for entirely free of charge *e)*.

**Andrew II**, King of **Hungary**, transferred this year to Brother **Ponce**, Preceptor of the Kingdom, the supervision and guarding of **Klissa Castle**, which sat upon the summit of a hill in **Dalmatia**, with the condition that he should garrison it with knights of his Order. They also possessed the fortress of **Urana** in Dalmatia, where the treasure of King Andrew was kept *f)*.

In the region of **Gallura** in **Sardinia**, the **Bishop of Saluzzo** consecrated the high altar of a church belonging to the Order around this time. This is now a collegiate church <note>original: "Kollegialkirche," a church where the ministry is performed by a "college" or community of canons rather than a single priest</note> *g)*.

After various unsuccessfully repeated attacks, the Crusaders despaired of capturing the tower through the means used thus far, until a Canon of Cologne <note>This refers to Oliver of Paderborn (c. 1170–1227), a chronicler and strategist who is historically credited with designing the successful siege engine at Damietta.</note>, who had recognized the deficiencies of the first wooden tower, proposed to erect an even stronger one, which would be high enough to reach and sweep <note>In military terms, "to sweep" means to fire upon the enemy from a superior height.</note> the top of the Taphnis <term>Taphnis: also known as the Tower of Chains, this was a massive fortification in the middle of the Nile that protected the city of Damietta.</term>. The greatest difficulty was to find a ship of such width as to give the tower a base area proportionate to its height; they also succeeded in this by strongly fastening two of the largest flat-bottomed vessels together with ropes, and using beams and planks to create the required base area. 

Upon this movable foundation the framework was built, whose supports consisted of four of the largest mast-trees, which leaned imperceptibly toward one another, giving the tower the necessary proportion. After the necessary floors, stairs, and openings were installed in its interior, a second base was erected on top, which was capable of carrying a smaller tower, the height of which was intended to surpass even the peak of the Taphnis. At the foot of this smaller tower, a drawbridge was attached, which could be raised or lowered at will, and also held suspended horizontally by means of two chains or ropes attached to the extreme ends. It was only toward the end of autumn that it became clear how much damage inactivity can cause during important undertakings. Terrible storms arose, which lasted for three days and three nights with such violence that the surging sea broke its banks and pushed against the flow of the Nile. The river then spread across the land and flooded the entire camp. Provisions, weapons, and baggage were all lost or ruined by the water, and one could catch fish from the sea and the Nile by hand inside the tents. Several ships sank, and four of the strongest were driven by the force of the water toward the city <note>The city refers to Damietta, the strategic port city in the Nile Delta currently under siege by the Crusaders.</note> and were burned by the enemy before the very eyes of the Christians.

This city, which formerly lay on the shore of the sea, is now several miles distant from it, either because it was rebuilt further inland, or because perhaps the sea has receded. It had twenty-two gates and was surrounded on one side by a double wall, and on the other by a triple wall. Upon their entry, the victors beheld devastation and objects of terror and pity everywhere. The half-rotted corpses lay in heaps in the streets, unburied, and the stench of decay was so overwhelming <note>original: unaufhaltsam; literally "unstoppable" or "irresistible," here referring to the pervasive smell.</note> that they almost turned back. The number of the sick amounted to nearly ten thousand, many of whom lay in a bed alongside the deceased and half-decomposed because they were too weak to carry them away. The provisions <note>original: Mundvorrath</note> were almost entirely consumed, but in terms of furniture, goods, and valuables, the booty was immeasurable. Among eighty thousand people, both citizens and soldiers, barely three hundred prominent men were to be found who could ransom themselves. As soon as the victors had inspected this scene of misery and horror, the infectious air and the smell of corpses forced them back into their camp. The Emperor furthermore promised that if he were to die before this crossing, or if the journey had to be canceled, this sum should only be used according to the judgment of the Grand Masters of the Temple and the Hospital <note>The Knights Hospitaller.</note>, who were to distribute and utilize it for the benefit of the Holy Land according to the advice of wise and experienced persons.

# Peter von Montaigu <note>Grand Master of the Knights Templar from 1218 to 1232.</note>

To enable the King to undertake this crusade, the clergy allocated one hundred thousand livres <note>The *livre* was the currency of France at the time.</note> from their revenues to him, as well as a tithe <term>tithe</term> <note>A ten-percent tax on income or produce, traditionally given to the church but here redirected for military use.</note> which he was permitted to levy on their estates for five years. As the deadline for Frederick to depart for Palestine approached once again, the Pope urged him to fulfill his vow and, in the meantime, had the crusade preached in England and Germany. However, these poor people, who were not accustomed to the fiery sky of Apulia, died by the thousands or returned to their homelands sick. Nonetheless, a considerable fleet was assembled and set sail in August.

But these poor people, who were not accustomed to the fiery sky of Apulia, died there by the thousands or returned to their homeland sick. Nevertheless, a considerable fleet was assembled, which set sail in August.

After the Templars had retaken their plunder from the Saracens, amounting to six thousand marks of silver, his lieutenant, the Count of Acerra <note>Thomas of Aquino, a loyal diplomat and military leader for Frederick II in Southern Italy.</note>, had snatched it back from them by force and given it back to the infidels, in the hope that these knights, by virtue of their order's statutes, would not be permitted to defend themselves against him <note>The Templar Rule generally prohibited members from striking fellow Christians, especially those representing legitimate authority, a restriction the Count attempted to exploit to seize their assets.</note>. The same commander had taken various lands from both orders and had wanted to destroy their privileges in order to subject them to imperial power. The Emperor had returned one hundred slaves to the Saracens, which these knights had in Sicily and Apulia, without compensating them for it, etc. z).

# History of the Templars. Book Seven.

This was the Pope's view of the Emperor's conduct at that time. Frederick had previously declared publicly that he would undertake the defense of the Holy Land as a Templar rather than as an Emperor—meaning he was willing to sacrifice everything for the cause. However, he later proved that he was no slave to his own word; for as soon as he heard of the events in Apulia <note>A region in Southern Italy. While Frederick was on crusade, Papal forces—often called the "Soldiers of the Keys"—had invaded his Sicilian territories, forcing him to conclude his campaign in the East hastily.</note>, he hurried to reach a settlement with Meleddin <note>Al-Kamil, the Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt (r. 1218–1238), nephew of Saladin.</note>. According to some historians, he employed certain means in doing so that were entirely unworthy of His Majesty <note>original: "Sr. Majestät"</note> a).

<margin>1229</margin> The Sultan was well informed of all these disturbances and difficulties, and was consequently less inclined to yield. At last, he allowed himself to be persuaded, and a secret settlement was reached, containing the following articles:

> 1) "The Emperor was to receive Jerusalem in its current state and could rebuild its walls at his pleasure, with the exception, however, of the Temple (or the mosque built on the site of Solomon's Temple <note>This refers to the Temple Mount, specifically the Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa Mosque, which remained under Muslim religious control despite the city returning to Christian hands.</note>), which, along with its surrounding grounds, was to remain with the Muslims. Furthermore, no Christian should venture inside who had not accepted the Muhammadan faith."

> 2) "Pilgrimages to the Holy Sepulchre and Bethlehem would remain permitted to Christians, and the latter city, as well as Nazareth and Thoron <note>A major Crusader castle in modern-day Lebanon, also known as Tibnin.</note>..."

3) "During the ten-year truce, every citizen of Jerusalem, whether Christian or Muslim, was to be judged and governed solely by the leaders of his own nation. This treaty was sworn by both sides on the 18th of February. Of the military orders, the Teutonic Knights <note>original: "deutschen Herren." Unlike the Templars and Hospitallers, this order was closely tied to the Holy Roman Emperors.</note> were the only ones to participate, as the Templars and Hospitallers considered it disadvantageous and dishonorable. They represented to the Emperor that the honor of the Franks <note>A term used by both Middle Eastern and Western chroniclers to refer to the Western European Crusaders.</note> was all the more at stake here because one could not only strip the infidels of everything they possessed in Syria, but also, due to the discord prevailing among them, conquer their very states. Furthermore, they argued that this peace could not be lasting because the young Sultan of Damascus <note>An-Nasir Dawud, the nephew of Al-Kamil (Meleddin). The Ayyubid Empire was often fractured by internal family rivalries.</note>, Meleddin’s nephew, did not approve of the surrender of Jerusalem, arguing that his uncle had no right to do so; consequently, the nephew would always be able to resume the war against the Christians.

### History of the Templars. Seventh Book.

Indeed, the young Sultan <note>An-Nasir Dawud, the nephew of Al-Kamil who ruled Damascus.</note> revoked everything his uncle had promised and prepared to prove to him that he no longer required such a guardian; however, neither his threats nor the representations of the Knights could prevent the conclusion of the settlement. The Emperor received all the aforementioned castles and territories, and after the Muslims had left Jerusalem—except for those who guarded the Temple—a multitude of Christian families and monks moved back there. It is claimed that Frederick left the territory and the perimeter of the Temple to the Muslims only to prevent the Knights Templar <term>Tempelherrn</term> from reclaiming their original residence, which stood right next to the Temple <note>The "Temple" refers to the Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, which the Templars had used as their headquarters in the previous century.</note>. Montaigu's successor was a French knight who is mentioned in du Cange's <note>Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange (1610–1688), a distinguished French philologist and historian of the Middle Ages.</note> list of Grand Masters only by his initials. ### History of the Templars. Eighth Book.

The Templars, who had reason enough to make common cause with him <note>Referring to the local opposition against the Emperor's officials</note>, set aside their hatred for the Emperor <note>Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor</note> for the sake of the common good and sought, as much as possible, to calm the tempers of the people once more.

The Emperor's Marshal <note>Richard Filangieri, the Emperor's representative in the East</note> had already been defeated in a skirmish when the two Grand Masters <note>The leaders of the Templars and the Hospitallers</note> offered their mediation and departed from Beirut <note>Baruth</note>, which the Germans held. Here they offered proposals for a settlement and formal representations. ### History of the Templars. Book Eight.

Around this same time, another dispute arose between the Order and the city of Marseille, because the knights held the right to pay no duties or taxes there for their ships and similar matters. However, when Marseille changed its form of government and introduced a republican constitution, these rights were taken away from the knights. They turned to the Constable <note>A high-ranking military and administrative official</note> of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, Odo of Montbéliard, and demanded that he seize the goods and ships of the Marseillais in the port of Acre <note>Also known as Akkon; the primary port and capital of the later Crusader Kingdom</note>. Odo brought about a settlement between the two parties, by which the knights were permitted, twice a year—in March and August—to load their ships in the port of Marseille, to embark everything without taxes, and to carry up to fifteen hundred pilgrims without paying any fees for them, except for any merchants who might be traveling with them *c)*. <margin>1235</margin> They were no more successful with the King of England when they presented him with the injustices committed by his officials in Gascony <note>A region in southwestern France then held by the English crown</note>. Henry <note>King Henry III</note> was too sluggish to take serious action against these oppressions, and the Gascons revolted in the year 1240. Henry’s officials there were in such a dire state that the Templars were forced to take over the collection of royal funds for a period of time *e)*.

Nowhere at that time was the Order wealthier than in England, and one is rightly astonished when reading of the grants, privileges, and freedoms bestowed upon them in this kingdom. The knights of the New Temple in London <note>The headquarters of the Templars in England</note> were responsible for guarding the Chancery <note>The office responsible for the production of official government documents</note> and the royal funds; the Preceptor <note>The head of the Order within a particular province or region</note> of the Order in England held a seat and a vote in Parliament on the first bench. Furthermore, they held the right of sanctuary for their houses, as well as high and low jurisdiction <note>The legal right to judge both minor disputes and serious crimes, including those carrying the death penalty</note> across all their estates. They were exempt from all taxes, levies, tolls, and so forth, and could buy and sell without paying the slightest fee, unlike all other subjects. Henry III not only confirmed all these freedoms but also added new ones, the listing of which would be too extensive here.

While the Franciscan monks <note>original: "Barfüßer Mönche," literally "Barefoot monks," a common name for the Franciscans due to their simple dress</note> and other orders traversed Europe to announce indulgences and preach the Crusade <note>original: "das Kreuz zu predigen," literally "to preach the cross," referring to the recruitment of crusaders</note>, the knight Thomas traveled from Rome to England with authority from the Holy See to convert the vow to fight the Saracens <note>A term used in the Middle Ages to refer to Muslims</note> into money. To be sure, the Pope made every conceivable effort to prove that this served the greatest advantage of the Christians in the East <note>The Crusader States in the Levant</note>, but no one wanted to believe it, and the Easterners grumbled loudly about it *g)*.

## Seventeenth Grand Master.

# Herman of Périgord.

The position that Herman assumed was dangerous and far from enviable; in the East, the Order was without support, and in Naples and Sicily, it had been stripped of its estates. Everywhere, the Order was persecuted and deprived of its rights by the Emperor <note>Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, who was frequently at odds with the papacy and the military orders</note>, King Béla of Hungary, and Béla’s brother Coloman, Duke of Slavonia. These latter two snatched away from the knights what their ancestors had gifted to the Order, without paying the slightest heed to the threats of the Pope, who menaced them with all his severity *i*).

Under these circumstances, Herman departed from Sicily, and he had hardly arrived in the East when he was forced to march against the Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslim forces</note>, who had attacked the fort of Guaskam <note>Also known as Bagras or Gaston, a strategic castle near the Syrian Gates</note> in the vicinity of Aleppo. He went to meet them with his knights and forced them to abandon the site. However, because the enemy was pursued too heatedly, the entire hostile army came to the aid of the fugitives. A bloody encounter then began, in which the knights were completely defeated and scattered; the Saracens themselves lost nearly three thousand men. Grand Master Herman could barely—

After this service rendered to the Hospitallers, Hermann and his knights joined with Bohemond V, Prince of Antioch, who had been insulted by the King of Armenia in the person of some of his subjects. This latter king was Hethum I <note>Reigned 1226–1270; he was a key figure in the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.</note>, the son-in-law and successor of King Leo <note>Leo I (or II), the first king of Cilician Armenia, who had a long-standing rivalry with the military orders.</note>, who had so often been in conflict with the Templars and had finally, in 1213, seemingly reconciled with them. Hethum hated the knights as much as his predecessors had, and when he learned they had threatened to march into Armenia to obtain justice for themselves, he ordered Bohemond's already mistreated subjects to be partly flogged and partly executed. # History of the Knights Templar. Book Eight.

The new crusade proceeded very slowly, due partly to the successful progress of the imperial arms in the Papal States <note>Conflicts between the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II and the Pope frequently diverted resources from the Holy Land.</note> and partly to the poor condition of Romania <note>A term used here to describe the Latin Empire of Constantinople.</note>. For this purpose, he received five hundred pounds from the King of England <note>Henry III.</note>, which the knights Richard Renger and Hugo Stockton, as administrators of the royal treasury, paid out to him. Saint Louis <note>Louis IX of France.</note> advanced him fifty thousand *livres Parisis* <note>A specific medieval French currency minted in Paris.</note> against the collateral of the County of Namur, the administration of which was entrusted to the Templars until the sum was repaid <gloss>z)</gloss>. The Pope <note>Gregory IX.</note>, though unable to assist him directly, arranged for a portion of the crusaders destined for Palestine to go to Constantinople instead. ### History of the Templars. Eighth Book.

Under the leadership of the Count of Bar and the Count of Montfort, they ventured ever further, and when they learned from a scout of the Templars that a corps of fifteen hundred Saracens had entrenched themselves near Gaza, they moved to attack them. The Crusaders, who had expected no resistance, were seized with terror and thought of flight; but the Saracens, who had meanwhile been reinforced, pursued them once more and surrounded them on all sides, so that only a few were able to escape. The Counts of Bar and Clermont, along with several other nobles, remained on the field, having fought with desperate bravery until the end. Count Montfort, the entire infantry, and some knights of both orders <note>Referring to the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller.</note>, who had allowed themselves to be reluctantly swept along with the others, were taken prisoner and brought to Cairo *w)*.

### History of the Templars. Book Eight.

The Templars were opposed to the views of the English Crusaders; they collected money in England intended for the Crusades and sent it out of the country. This was enough to provoke the ire of the English monk Paris <note>Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259), a Benedictine monk of St. Albans known for his colorful but often biased historical accounts</note>, whom even his own editor describes as a prejudiced and blind judge *l)*.

He depicts Saint Louis <note>King Louis IX of France (r. 1226–1270), later canonized as a saint</note> sometimes as an unjust man, and at other times as cruel and godless *m)*; and because King John <note>John "Lackland" (r. 1199–1216)</note> seized the assets of his abbey, Saint Albans, he portrayed him as a madman, an apostate, and a despiser of religion who supposedly sent an embassy to the Miramolin <note>original: "Miramolin"; a corruption of the title *Amir al-Mu'minin*, the "Commander of the Faithful," referring here to the Almohad Caliph in North Africa</note> of Africa with the intention of adopting the Muslim faith *n)*. ### History of the Templars. Eighth Book.

From Hungary, the Tatars <note>The Mongol forces, frequently called "Tatars" in medieval European chronicles</note> moved <unclear>through</unclear> Sweden, Russia, and Persia all the way to the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea. There, they drove the Khwarazmians <note>A nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia whose empire had been dismantled by the Mongols</note>, a fierce Asian people, out of their possessions. These people, not knowing where to flee to escape the Tatars, turned to the Sultan of Egypt and requested that he assign them land where they could settle. The Sultan paid little heed to the agreement <note>Likely referring to the truce established during the Barons' Crusade</note> he had concluded with the Hospitallers <note>The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem</note>, the troops of the Emperor, and the remaining Christians in the Orient. He received the Khwarazmians favorably and proposed that they march to Palestine and settle there, promising to protect them against all enemies. His intention was to use them to corner the Sultan of Damascus and his allies, the Templars.

Now the Khwarazmians, joined by the Egyptians and numbering twenty thousand cavalry, set out against the Christians, who barely had time to recognize the danger. The army invaded the territory of Jerusalem from the direction of Tiberias, and everything they encountered was plundered, burned, and destroyed.

Now the advantage of the agreement with the Sultan of Damascus was finally realized; the Hospitallers united with the Templars and <unclear>them</unclear> and the other Sultans who were concerned <unclear>by the situation</unclear>.

### Eighteenth Grand Master.

## William of Sonnak

<margin>1247</margin> In this highly precarious situation, the assembled chapter elected an elderly man from Languedoc, **William of Sonnak** (or **Sernay**), as Grand Master. He had made himself famous through his great insight, his irreproachable morals, and his zeal for the Order.

### History of the Templars. Ninth Book. ###

"...never again receive such deputations without his express consent." Given the manner in which the Sultan received the emissaries who wished to ransom their captured brothers—where certainly no secret understanding between the Grand Master and him could be imagined—it is probable that the Templars and other knights did not wish to see such a formidable enemy provoked under the pretext of a new Crusade. This was because the newly arrived troops always returned home after a few attempts, leaving the entire weight of the war on the shoulders of the knightly orders and the other inhabitants of the East <margin>f)</margin> <note>original: "Morgenländern"; a historical term for the peoples of the Levant and Middle East</note>.

At the end of May, Louis <note>King Louis IX of France, later canonized as Saint Louis</note> put to sea again, having previously sent a declaration of war to the Sultan of Egypt. The entire fleet arrived within six days from Limassol <note>original: "Limisso," a port city in Cyprus</note> at the shores of Damietta <note>original: "Damiate," a crucial port city on the Nile Delta</note>. The fleet consisted of eighteen hundred large and small vessels, yet in the entire army, there were only two thousand eight hundred knights along with their attendants. The enemy awaited them on the shore; nevertheless, the anchors were dropped, and the King and his commanders threw themselves into the water with unparalleled intrepidity. The soldiers followed this example, and so they waded to the shore under a continuous rain of arrows, chased the enemy back to the gates of the city, and took possession of it two days later without a single stroke of the sword, even though it was one of the strongest fortresses in Egypt. Around this time, the English Templars had a dispute with Robert, Bishop of Lincoln <note>This refers to Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), a famous English statesman and theologian who often clashed with the military orders and the papacy.</note>, which was later settled by Innocent IV *l)*. The King received them kindly, gave them gifts, and sent them back more satisfied with him than with the Grand Masters.

Shortly after, the King wished to attempt an expedition against Naplouse <note>The city of Nablus in present-day Palestine.</note> and disclosed this to the commanders and the Templars. The latter replied that they would be responsible for its success, but since the undertaking was dangerous, they asked him not to join the march. The King insisted on it, and the matter fell through *o)*. Some time later, he proposed the siege of Belinas <note>Banyas, a strategic site at the foot of Mount Hermon, anciently known as Caesarea Philippi.</note>, and this too was approved, but under the previous condition. The King gave in and stayed home. Now the Templars, Hospitallers, and the Royal troops attacked the place with such impetuosity that the enemy abandoned everything and retreated into the mountains. Belinas was surrendered almost without a single blow of the sword.

Immediately in the first year of his accession to the throne, he issued a bull <note>A formal proclamation or decree issued by a Pope, named after the "bulla" or lead seal attached to it.</note> in which he: 1) threatened with harsh punishment all those who would demand tithes <note>A ten-percent tax on agricultural produce or income, traditionally paid to the local church.</note> from them; 2) commanded the bishops to accept the clergymen who were presented to them by the Preceptors <note>A high-ranking official in the Templar Order who governed a specific province or estate.</note> for service in the Order's churches, without the Knights being required to assign a preliminary salary to these clergymen. In this year, the Grand Master **Reinald** died after a six-year reign. The term *Magister* <note>Latin for "Master."</note> led Father **Berthollet** w) astray, causing him to name a certain **Fulco of Saint Michel** as the successor—an error into which several others followed him.

# History of the Knights Templar. Tenth Book.

Louis the Saint <note>Louis IX of France (reigned 1226–1270), known for his piety and his participation in the Seventh and Eighth Crusades.</note> deposited into the Templar treasury in Paris the three thousand seven hundred and twenty pounds that he owed to the King of England. At the same time, Henry III saw himself forced to pawn the diamonds of his crown to French merchants and sent them to Queen Margaret <note>Margaret of Provence, wife of Louis IX and sister to Eleanor, the wife of Henry III.</note>, his sister-in-law, to be deposited as a pledge in the Templar treasury. The treasurer of the Temple House in Paris, Knight Peter Bostelli, received them, locked them in two chests, and handed the keys to the English ambassador n).

This trust from the regents and the office of treasurer, which they held in Paris and London, brought them much trouble and many persecutions.

<margin>1262</margin> In this year, Henry III of England won over the commander of the Tower of London and seized all the money he found there. In the following year, as he could neither pay his troops nor disband them, he employed the same means; he arrived unexpectedly in London with a troop of armed men, broke into the Temple court <note>The New Temple in London, which functioned as one of the most secure "banks" in the medieval world.</note>, and took ten thousand pounds sterling which the citizens of London had deposited there. This act of violence caused a general but fruitless grumbling o).

# William of Beaujeu.

The Bishop of Tripoli fled to the Templars, and they immediately received orders to evacuate the city and the county. ### History of the Knights Templar. Tenth Book.

In the year <margin>1286</margin>, which was the first year of the reign of Philip the Fair <note>Philip IV of France, who would later become the Order's primary antagonist</note>, they were still so highly esteemed in France that the Preceptor <term>A high-ranking regional administrator of the Order</term> of France held a seat and a vote in the Parliament <note>The Parlement of Paris, at this time the supreme judicial body of the French kingdom</note> alongside the counts, bishops, and prelates *h)*.

They were still in full enjoyment of all their privileges, and the clergy watched closely to ensure they did not exceed them. The nobility continued to destine their sons for the Order and to enrich it with donations. Although the knights were exempt from the obligation of hosting bishops, they nevertheless occasionally consented to do so, and among others, they received the Archbishop of Burgos with many honors *i)*. Several favors granted to the Order and the names of their benefactors can be read in the writers cited below *k)*.

In Alsace, there were three Temple estates <note>original: "Tempelhöfe," referring to commanderies or administrative manors</note> at that time: one between Bergheim and Ribeauvillé <note>original: "Bertheim und Rappotsweiler"</note>, another at Dorlisheim, and the third at Baumgarten *l)*.

### Eleventh Book.

## William of Beaujeu.

The new King of Cyprus <note>Henry II of Lusignan, the last crowned King of Jerusalem to reside in the Levant</note> made a bold resolution in 1286 to support the Holy Land once more, and appeared with a fine fleet off the coast of Acre. This arrival was all the more welcome as the people saw themselves abandoned by the Pope and the other reigning monarchs. The governor representing King Charles of Sicily <note>Charles I of Anjou, who had previously purchased the title to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, leading to a dynastic dispute</note> saw clearly that any resistance here would be in vain; he withdrew into the citadel, where he was forced to surrender after a few days. Following this, Lusignan had himself crowned King of Jerusalem.

The indifference with which the Knights <note>The Templars, who remained neutral during this particular transition of power</note> allowed this to happen would later cost them dearly. As soon as the son of King Charles of Sicily <note>Charles II of Naples, also known as Charles the Lame</note>—whom the King of Aragon had been holding captive—was set free, he seized everything the Order possessed within his states under the pretext that the Knights had acted unlawfully against him. Later, in the year 1307 <note>The year the Templars were arrested across France</note>, he became one of the most eager to strike at their property in Provence. And yet, the Templars could not have acted otherwise; whether they had declared themselves for or against the King of Cyprus, they would have brought a dangerous enemy upon themselves in either case.

Meanwhile, the deputies of the two Grand Masters <note>the leaders of the Templars and the Hospitallers</note> returned to the Orient and brought little comfort with them. However, people remained calm because the truce was being strictly observed by both sides, and so everything went well until the Pope's auxiliary troops—or rather, the band of robbers from Italy—arrived. These men disregarded everything; they attacked the Muslims <note>original: "Muselmänner"</note> who, under the protection of the truce, were bringing provisions to the Christians, plundering them and slaying nineteen of them. Now the Sultan swore that he would level Acre <note>original: "Akkon"</note> to the ground just as he had done to Tripoli. In October 1290, he set out from Cairo with sixty thousand cavalry and one hundred and forty thousand infantry, but he died on the way and recommended the continuation of the enterprise to his son Khalil <note>Al-Ashraf Khalil</note>. # History of the Templars. Eleventh Book. #

<margin>1291</margin> of the following year, he arrived before Acre <note>modern-day Akko</note> and began to besiege it.

The Franks <note>A collective term used in the Middle East at the time to describe all Western European Crusaders</note> lacked not only money but, what was even worse, unity. Everyone wanted to command, and no one wanted to obey; the garrison, which consisted of eighteen thousand men, was a chaotic mixture of people from all nations who knew neither common customs nor military discipline. Finally, dire necessity forced them to transfer the supreme command to the Grand Master Beaujeu <note>Guillaume de Beaujeu, the 21st Grand Master of the Templars</note>. He made every possible preparation for a stubborn resistance, but the King of Cyprus <note>Henry II of Jerusalem and Cyprus</note> was the first to falter; instead of supporting the German knights <note>original: "deutschen Ritter"; the Teutonic Order</note>, he secretly sailed away with three thousand men. On May 18th, the Sultan risked a major assault and broke into the city, where every step of his progress had to be bought with blood. Beaujeu advised the Grand Master of the Hospitallers <note>the Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem</note> to invade the enemy's camp to lure the Sultan's forces away, but his path was cut off. In the meantime, Beaujeu himself was killed by a poisoned arrow, after having seen most of his knights fall before his eyes. Now the Franks fled in all directions: one part toward the sea, the other toward the Temple castle <term>the Citadel; the fortified headquarters of the Templars in the city</term>, where they entrenched themselves, while the Muslims <note>original: "Muselmänner"</note> in the city devastated everything with fire and sword. A portion of those who tried to swim to the ships drowned because the sea was very rough, and the Patriarch <note>Nicholas of Hanapes, the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem</note> took such a great number of people into his boat that it foundered, and he drowned along with everyone on board.

## Twenty-second Grand Master.

# Gaudini.

<margin>1291</margin> After Beaujeu’s death, Gaudini <note>Thibaud Gaudin, the 22nd Grand Master of the Templars, who presided over the Order's final days in the Holy Land</note>, surnamed "the Monk," was elected Grand Master. The Grand Master sent word to the Sultan once more to explain the situation, but Khalil <note>Al-Ashraf Khalil, the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> had the deputies beheaded, and now there was no other salvation but flight. The Grand Master successfully escaped during the night, rescuing the treasure of the Order, his own adornments, and the holy relics. It is estimated that forty thousand Christians were either killed or taken into captivity that day; of five hundred Templars <term>members of the Order of the Temple</term>, only the ten who accompanied the Grand Master escaped. The Sultan had the city plundered, set on fire at its four corners, and razed everything to the ground.

History of the Templars. Book Eleven.

### Twenty-third Grand Master.
## Jacques de Molay.

<margin>1298</margin> The last Grand Master was the man known to all historians as Jacques de Molay—and not "Molai," as Du Cange <note>Charles du Fresne, Sieur du Cange, a prominent 17th-century historian and linguist</note> claims *b)*. This man was once so highly esteemed at the court of France that he stood as godfather for one of King Philip's children *c)*.

Now, disputes arose between the King of Cyprus <note>Henry II of Jerusalem and Cyprus</note> and the Templars. The King feared they might become too powerful through their many possessions; he stripped them of some of their privileges in his land, subjected their subordinates to a poll tax of two <term>bezants</term> <note>A gold or silver coin originally from the Byzantine Empire, widely used as a standard currency in the medieval Mediterranean</note>, and forbade them from purchasing further estates or even the continued construction of their houses. Now <margin>1299</margin> frequent complaints reached Rome, and Boniface <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note> took them up very earnestly, making representations, pleading, and finally threatening *d)*; but all was in vain. King Lusignan continued to oppress his people, the nobility, and the clergy so severely that his brothers, especially Aimery <note>Original: Almerich; he later became the usurping Governor of Cyprus</note>, undertook to depose him.

*c)* Boccaccio, Bzovius, cited in Friedrich Spanheim’s *Introduction to Sacred History* <note>original Latin: "introd. in hist. Sacram"</note>, p. 455.

# Jacques de Molay.

Already in the year 1298, the Muslims <note>original: "Muselmänner"</note> had invaded Antioch and had forced King Leo <note>Leo II (or III) of Cilician Armenia, a key ally of the Crusader states</note> to entrench himself in the highlands until his brother-in-law, the Khan of the Tatars, Ghazan <note>original: "Gazan," the Mongol ruler of the Ilkhanate</note>, could come to his aid. In this year, Ghazan appeared with two hundred thousand riders, and it seemed as if everything would take a favorable turn for the Christians once again. The Sultan of Egypt, Melek-Nazar <note>Al-Nasir Muhammad, the Mamluk Sultan</note>, was defeated, and Ghazan sent a delegation to the Pope and the Western princes to ask them for support. But in Europe, people were occupied with other matters, and the delegates received little or no hearing.

Ghazan, meanwhile, had to return home due to internal unrest and left twenty thousand Tatars with the Christians, whereupon they captured Damascus and Jerusalem for a short time and celebrated the Easter festival in the latter city for the last time.

### History of the Templars. Eleventh Book.

The Templars gave proof of their loyalty to Philip <note>Philip IV, known as Philip the Fair</note> on this occasion, in that their Grand Visitor **Hugh of Peralda** <note>also known as Hugues de Pairaud, a high-ranking official of the Order in France</note>, at a general assembly where it was decided to oppose the undertakings of the Roman court <note>the Papacy</note>, joined with the abbots of the Cistercians, Premonstratensians, and the Abbot of Cluny to appeal to a future Pope regarding Boniface’s conduct toward Philip *f)*.

His Chancellor **Nogaret** <note>Guillaume de Nogaret, Philip’s chief minister and a key figure in the downfall of the Order</note> was their most implacable enemy because, according to some, they had handed over his father—or according to others, his grandfather—to the Inquisition, which had him sentenced to death as a heretic *h)*.

The council of King Philip consisted at that time of the following persons, whose descriptions we borrow from Mezerai <note>François Eudes de Mézeray, a prominent 17th-century French historian</note>. Philip immediately invited the Archbishop to a meeting at an abbey near Saint-Jean-d'Angély, where, after they had sworn loyalty to one another, Philip offered to make him Pope if he promised to fulfill six conditions. Beside himself with joy, the Archbishop threw himself at the King’s feet and promised to fulfill everything he demanded. The King raised him up and demanded the following five points <note>Though the text initially mentions six points, it begins listing them here; the final point was often kept secret in historical accounts of this meeting</note>: 1) that he should reconcile the King with the Church and forgive the wrong the King had done to Boniface. 2) That he should lift the excommunication <note>original: *Bann*</note> and all other ecclesiastical penalties that the King and his followers had incurred.

The authorities were to, as soon as they received the order, discreetly inquire into the number of Templar estates in each district, and even into the possessions of the rest of the clergy, so that it would appear as if they were coming merely on account of a new tithe <term>tithe|A tax, historically one-tenth of annual produce or earnings, paid to support the church</term>.

Then the knights were to be arrested, imprisoned individually, and their properties immediately managed by others. The inquisitors <note>Ecclesiastical judges appointed to investigate and suppress heresy</note> were then to assemble and, if necessary, make use of torture during their interrogations.

->## Jacques de Molay. ##<-

Those criminals who confessed were to be promised mercy and pardon; otherwise, they were to be condemned to death. First, an oath was to be demanded from them that they would tell the truth, and then they were to be questioned skillfully <note>original: "adroitement," meaning cleverly or with dexterity</note> about their reception into the Order and their vows; in this, initially, only general terms were to be used until the truth was learned from them.

The articles about which they were to be interrogated are the same as those already mentioned above, except that a magic belt <note>Accusations often involved a "cord of secret power" allegedly worn by the knights after it had touched a mysterious idol</note> was added, as well as the accusation that their priests did not consecrate the Host <term>Host|The bread used in the Christian ceremony of the Eucharist or Mass, which is believed to be transformed into the body of Christ</term> during the Mass.

In a letter dated September 22nd, the Grand Inquisitor and confessor to the King, William of Paris, exhorts his fellow members, the Jacobins <term>Jacobins|A name used in France for the Dominican Order, known for their role as inquisitors</term>, to proceed with the investigation with the utmost severity g), which was superfluous for men of that sort, as all of France had long cried out against their cruelty, and Philip had even been forced long before to prescribe certain laws to restrain them h). Barbarism, ignorance, debauchery, and perjury were so common at that time that the church councils had to constantly issue laws against them and threaten punishments i).

The King’s plan to unite both orders <note>the Templars and the Hospitallers</note> and to place one of his sons at their head—who was also intended to become King of Jerusalem—had been thwarted by the opposition of Molay. Furthermore, Molay’s refusal to pay the tithes, to which the Order was not subject by virtue of its privileges; his insistence on the repayment of a sum which he had advanced for the wedding celebrations of Princess Isabelle n); and finally, the general rumors that the Order had brought immeasurable treasures back from the Orient—all of this, along with other reasons already mentioned, aroused suspicion regarding the true motives of the King and his ministers.

To dispel these suspicions, an assembly of canons and theologians was held the following day in the cathedral, before which Nogaret sought to justify the motives for these arrests and to uphold the accusations against the Order. At the same time, it was announced to the people by the sound of trumpets that they were to gather eight days later in the gardens of the <term>Palais Royal|The royal palace in Paris, the seat of the Kings of France</term> to hear a reading of the abominations of which the knights and the entire Order had been found guilty.

These were the main accusations, notwithstanding the fact that several more extensive lists of charges exist; however, all of them can be reduced to these eleven points, which are preserved in the Chronicle of Saint-Denis <note>A famous medieval historical record compiled by the monks of the Abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris.</note>.

The first point requires no refutation, because it belongs to God alone to judge our faith. The latter part of that charge can be explained very naturally in the following way. It was, namely, an old custom of all military orders to dub the new recruits as knights <note>original: "Ritterschlag"</note>, provided this had not already been done by a prince or a king. The admission of the Templars took place publicly, but the dubbing to knighthood occurred behind closed doors; this was not forbidden by any law at the time and was generally known. <page-num>204</page-num>

# History of the Knights Templar. Twelfth Book. #

At the same time as Philip <note>King Philip IV of France, known as "the Fair."</note> wrote to the Pope, he sent one of his confidants, Bernard Peleti, to the new King Edward of England <note>Edward II, who had recently ascended the throne in 1307.</note>, with the invitation to proceed against the Order in the same manner as he had. Edward replied on October 30th that he had shared the letter with the counts, prelates, and nobles of his council, but no one could be convinced of the truth of the unheard-of accusations. At the same time, the King's council issued a letter of defense for the knights to the Kings of Portugal and Aragon, and to those of Castile and Sicily, in which they were warned not to give ear to such slanders. A similar letter was sent to the Pope f).

This letter might perhaps have had some effect on the Pope, but it arrived precisely at a time when he was at Poitiers <note>The city where Pope Clement V resided at the time, as the papacy was under heavy French influence.</note> renewing his promise to the King, and where both were consulting with one another on how the other European princes could be moved to follow France's example. The Pope assigned the draft of a circular <note>A formal letter intended for wide distribution to other rulers.</note> drawn up for that purpose, and the King, who had already anticipated him, was so delighted to be able to confirm his claims through the testimony of the Pope that the letter was immediately prepared and sent around to all the courts of Europe. In Languedoc, they had already been rounded up the previous year. In Beaucaire, from which Nogaret <note>Guillaume de Nogaret, the powerful advisor to King Philip IV of France and a primary architect of the Order's downfall.</note> drew his income, sixty of them were taken prisoner, among whom were five knights and one priest; the others were serving brothers, servants, and so on. Almost all confessed to some of the accusations and denied the rest, primarily the worship of an image <note>original: "Bildes" — referring to the "Baphomet" or idol the Templars were accused of worshipping.</note> and the desecration of the Sacrament. They also confessed that <term>sodomy</term> <note>In this historical context, "sodomy" was a broad legal and religious term for non-procreative sexual acts, used as a standard accusation to justify the suppression of the Order.</note> had been permitted to them, but all denied that they had ever made use of this permission. After this interrogation, they were given eight days of reflection to confess further, and the two Inquisitors—two Jacobin monks <note>original: "Jakobinermönche" — a common French term for the Dominican Order, who often served as Inquisitors.</note>—offered to hear their confessions k). The end and final fate of these men is also unknown.

It is not exactly known how the knights fared in the Netherlands, yet this much is certain: they were pursued as far as the County of Zeeland <note>A coastal province in the southwestern Netherlands.</note>. This was carried out, and only two, who happened to be absent at the time, escaped.

All of this would have been sufficient if the intention were merely to punish them, but the goal was to utterly destroy the entire Order. To excuse himself somewhat to the Pope, Philip <note>King Philip IV of France, also known as Philip the Fair, who was the primary instigator of the Templars' downfall.</note> held various assemblies of theologians, the first of which took place on March 25th in *Paris*, and the second in *Tours* during May. All these gentlemen—some voluntarily, others under duress—approved of the King's conduct in the present case; those who refused to appear, however, were condemned to pay a fine l). The majority of the judges condemned the knights to death, but the Parisian theological faculty, when asked for its opinion on the matter, replied that one must adhere to the judgment of the Roman court <note>The Papal Curia or the Pope’s administrative apparatus.</note>, to which alone it belonged to judge such crimes m).

Equipped with these testimonies, the King traveled to *Poitiers* and demanded of the Pope—

# Book Thirteen.

## Jacques de Molay.

<margin>1308</margin>
Up to this point, the knights had still counted on the great services they had rendered to Christendom and on the goodwill of the highest authorities, but the bull *Granting Mercy* <note>original Latin: "faciens Misericordiam"</note>, which dishonored them in the eyes of all Europe, crushed all their hopes. To forestall the storm in *Cyprus*, where the governor <term>Statthalter: a high-ranking official or regent acting as a representative of a sovereign</term> *Amalric*, as we have seen, was already unfavorably disposed toward them, fifteen of the most prominent knights went to him in *Nicosia* on May 27th and declared that, out of respect for the Holy See, they were ready to submit to whatever the governor would decree regarding their property and their persons u). This availed them nothing; *Amalric* had them disarmed, taken prisoner, guarded individually, and confiscated their property. However, they were not treated with as much severity as elsewhere, as there were still Templars in *Cyprus* even during the reign of Pope John XXII <note>John XXII was Pope from 1316 to 1334, suggesting the suppression took longer to fully implement on the island</note>.

Gautier von Clifton. The most essential part of his statement was that they were never permitted to go to sleep without linen undergarments and belts <note>the "girdle" of chastity mentioned on the previous page</note>, were not allowed to stay in the house of a woman in childbirth <note>a restriction intended to maintain the brothers' ritual purity and strict distance from domestic or secular family life</note>, and could attend no christening or wedding feast. The Grand Master, as well as the other superiors—both clergy and laymen—could absolve <term>Absolution: the formal forgiveness of sins, usually a power reserved for ordained priests</term> their brothers of all sins, except for murder and the physical abuse of a priest. To the question of where they obtained their statutes <term>Statutes: the internal laws and regulations governing the Order's life and duties</term>, it was said: from the Preceptor <note>a high-ranking regional commander</note> of England; he received them from the Preceptor of France, and the latter from the Grand Master. Throughout the whole Order, there was likely only one and the same exception everywhere. The Grand Master was said to have given absolution in the following manner:

> "In the name of God, Saint Peter, and the Pope, I remit all types of sins for you,"

then he would have instructed a priest of the Order to perform the rest; those sins for which absolution is reserved for the Pope alone <note>certain grave sins in the medieval church required direct papal intervention for forgiveness</note> were likely excluded from this d).

This is everything that could be learned from the Scottish Templars. The ambiguity regarding the point of absolution arises because the defendants made no distinction in their statements between sacramental and general absolution <note>The inquisitors were looking for "sacramental" absolution—the forgiveness of sins against God—which laymen were forbidden to perform. The Templars may have been referring to "general" absolution, which was a remission of punishments for breaking the Order's own rules</note>.

# Jacques de Molay. #

In the absence of more knights, forty-two outside witnesses were interrogated, whose testimony was based mostly on suspicion. They believed, for example, that the Templars must be guilty because they kept their admissions secret and held their chapters <term>Chapter: a formal business and disciplinary meeting of the Order's members</term> at night; because they did not confess to the ordinary clergy; because they allowed no one into their chapter, absolved one another, and other such things. Most of them knew nothing at all <margin>e) <note>original: "Concilia magnae Brittanniae"; The Great Councils of Britain, Volume II, p. 382.</note></margin>. On the 19th, they were interrogated again regarding admissions, the chapter, confession, and so on, and they stood by their statements. Eight others who were interrogated on the 20th behaved in the same way. Most of these witnesses were acquaintances of the knights, tenants, serving brothers of the Order, and so forth. One of them said he had often stood at the altar and had not noticed that the priests of the Order consecrated the host <note>the bread used in the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> any differently than the rest of the clergy.

On November 25th, the national church council was opened in London, but because the knights stationed in York and Lincoln <note>original: "Linkolm"</note> had not yet been interrogated, it was decided not to take up the matter of the Templars until St. Matthias's Day <note>February 24th</note> of the following year.

They had been given neither time for reflection nor freedom for contemplation; consequently, all confessions against the Order were to be regarded as invalid. It was publicly known, he argued, that the King <note>Philip IV "the Fair" of France</note> had offered freedom, immunity from punishment, and even pensions to those who would testify against the Order; consequently, they had been bought and bribed. ...sessions from one day to the next, until the knights themselves rescued their judges from their embarrassment on the 29th of June. They declared once more that all the accusations were false and fabricated, but that they had already been so widely slandered <note>The German "verschrien" implies they had been "cried down" or made so infamous by rumor that a fair trial was impossible.</note> that it would be impossible for them to erase the general negative impression. They were immediately declared prisoners of the Church, whereas previously they had been considered prisoners of state, and the following day the final judgment for these twenty-four knights was pronounced: they were to spend the remainder of their days in the monasteries of the parish <note>While the text says "Kirchspiel" (parish), it refers here to the various religious houses within the wider Archbishopric of York.</note> of York.

# History of the Knights Templar. Fourteenth Book.

From all of this, one can see that Stapelbrugge sought only to save himself, whatever the cost. Regarding many other questions, he either issued denials or claimed he did not understand what was intended by them. Finally, he fell at their feet and begged for mercy with tears. In his case, the love of life triumphed over every other consideration.

On the 25th of June, Brother Tocei <note>B. Tocei; likely Thomas de Tocci or a similar variation of the name found in English trial records.</note>, who had likewise previously fled, was brought forward. This man begged for mercy right from the beginning, but steadfastly denied all charges except for the matter of absolution granted in the chapter <term>Chapter: a formal assembly or meeting of the members of a religious order to discuss business and discipline</term>. However, he made a distinction between sins and weaknesses. The former were punished with penance by the Order's priest, while the latter were handled by the superiors of the assembly. Since that time, two cases were excepted for which the Pope alone could grant absolution. He denied all the absurdities and shameful acts <note>This refers to the more salacious accusations of the trial, such as spitting on the cross or ritual sodomy.</note>; he admitted that the reception into the order was performed in secret, and that he had been told the devil took a knight at every chapter meeting. He had never seen "the head" <note>The "Idol Head" or Baphomet, which the Templars were famously accused of worshipping.</note>; they wore the cord <gloss>original: "Gürtel"</gloss> with good intentions; silence was imposed upon them; they were not permitted to confess to mendicant friars <term>Mendicant friars: members of religious orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans who lived by begging; the Templars were often forbidden from confessing to anyone outside their own Order</term>; unlawful gain was punished within the Order with the loss of the habit <gloss>original: "Ordenskleid"</gloss> and membership. He did not believe that Stapelbrugge had been received into the order twice, but he had been present at Stapelbrugge's reception fifteen years prior. When asked whether he approved of the confessions made by the other brothers, he said he did so only insofar as they were honorable men and his acquaintances.

# History of the Knights Templar. Fourteenth Book.

...confessed that fourteen days after his admission, he was led to the room of the Grand Master Molay at Garway <note>original: "Garwy"; a significant Templar estate and circular church in Herefordshire, England</note>, where he encountered two foreign knights and two serving brothers who guarded the door with swords in hand. The Grand Master questioned him regarding his initial reception and, upon receiving his answer, held a crucifix before him and asked whom this represented? To the answer that it was the Savior, who died for the sins of mankind, the Grand Master replied "that this was not true; Christ was born of a woman like other men and was executed because he called himself the Son of God; he himself had seen the place where he was born and crucified. This person he should now deny"—He had refused, but the threats of the Grand Master and the flashing swords had taught him to obey; however, he denied him only with his mouth. Thereupon he knelt down, asked for forgiveness for his faults, abjured his error, and was reconciled with the Church, just as Tocci and Stapelbrugge had been.

The Preceptor <term>Preceptor: A high-ranking officer in charge of a "Preceptory" or regional headquarters of the Order</term> William de la Moore and Imbert Blanke behaved quite differently. They declared that they could not confess to crimes and heresies they had never committed, and that no fear of man could move them to admit anything that ran contrary to the truth. As a reward for their steadfastness, both were taken to an even narrower prison until a new interrogation.

# Jacques de Molay.

Gradually, the majority of the prisoners adapted to the circumstances, yielded to their judges, admitted their guilt, and showed remorse for their committed or uncommitted faults, solely with the intention of being released from prison. They were all required to abjure <note>To "abjure" is to formally renounce a belief or claim under oath.</note>, and thus all the English Templars were reconciled with the Church, except for the three previously mentioned—who had confessed to certain *articles*—and five others whose confession of faith or abjuration was somewhat different. In the middle of September, the Pope <note>Pope Clement V, who was under significant pressure from King Philip IV of France.</note> traveled with the Cardinals to the upcoming general Church council <note>The Council of Vienne (1311–1312).</note>, where the matter of the Knights Templar was finally to be decided. Finally, the Pope dared to pose the question: whether it would not be advisable to abolish a society in which such abuses were so prevalent? The Fathers of the Council unanimously represented that such a distinguished society, which had rendered such great services to Christendom, should not be condemned unheard; they insisted that the path of legal justice must be followed with them. # Jakob von Molay.

...asserted the guilt of the Knights, and it was therefore not to be expected of them that they would pronounce the judgment upon the Order. It is also quite erroneously claimed that the Order was abolished by this <term>church assembly</term> <note>Referring to the Council of Vienne (1311–1312).</note>. The truth is this: The Pope withdrew with a small number of his devotees and abolished the Order on his own authority on the 22nd of March in a secret <term>consistory</term> <note>A private meeting of the Pope and his cardinals.</note> <margin>p)</margin>, destroying the same, as he himself confesses, not by rule of law, but out of precaution, and by virtue of the apostolic power, while reserving for himself the decision over its assets and persons. 

In the second session on the 3rd of April, the Pope made known to the entire assembly the abolition of the Order, which he had already decided twelve days prior. We find no traces in history that the assembly gave its consent orally or in writing; no one made a counter-representation, and since this silence was interpreted as consent, the words: *With the approval of the Holy Council* <note>original: "Sacro approbante Concilio"</note> were also inserted into the <term>bull of abolition</term> <note>The official papal document, titled "Vox in excelso," which suppressed the Order.</note>. Regarding the individuals of the <term>Knights</term> <note>The noble-born members of the Templar Order.</note>, the Pope reserved the judgment over some of them specifically for himself; the rest were left to the verdict of the provincial assemblies. Those found innocent were to be maintained from the assets of the Order according to their rank; those who confessed to something were to be treated with leniency, while those who confessed nothing—even under <term>torture</term>—were to be judged according to <term>canon law</term> <note>The internal legal system and ecclesiastical decrees of the Catholic Church.</note>; finally, the stubborn and the relapsed, who revoked their statements, were to be punished with all severity. All, except for these latter ones, were to be supported individually in monasteries using the Order's assets. Those who were still absent or fugitive were summoned to present themselves before their bishops within a year to await their judgment.

In Catalonia, the Knights had initially retreated to their fortified castles, but James II <note>James II of Aragon, who reigned from 1291 to 1327.</note> forced them to abandon these and handed them over to the Grand Inquisitor, who held them captive for five years. Tired of this imprisonment, the Knights finally appealed to the Archbishop of Tarragona, asking him to carry out the Pope’s command regarding them and to conduct an investigation into their lives and morals so that their case might finally reach a judgment. At this, toward the end of October, the Archbishop convened the bishops, prelates, abbots, priors, and others of his province. They investigated and interrogated the Knights and the witnesses, and since nothing could be proven against them, the verdict of the ecclesiastical assembly was that they—collectively and individually—were not guilty of the crimes, errors, and atrocities charged against them; for which reason they

This verdict, which silently condemned the Pope's <term>proceedings</term> <note>Pope Clement V had pushed for the Order's condemnation across Europe; the Catalan acquittal was a significant regional rejection of those charges.</note>, placed the Catalan bishops in no small embarrassment. It is quite erroneously asserted by Dupuy <note>Pierre Dupuy (1582–1651) was a French scholar whose history of the Templar trial was often seen as a defense of King Philip the Fair's actions.</note> that the Order of the Temple was abolished everywhere at that time, except in Germany, where the Knights supposedly prevented the publication of the <term>papal bull</term> <note>A formal public decree issued by the Pope, specifically the bull *Vox in excelso* (1312) which dissolved the Order.</note>. They maintained themselves for a while longer in the region of the Rhine, and the Archbishop of Mainz, who was tasked with carrying out the papal orders against them, permitted those in his province to transfer into the Teutonic Order <note>original: "Deutschen [Orden]"; a German crusading military order.</note> and the Order of the Hospitallers <note>original: "Hospitaliterorden"; also known as the Knights of Saint John, who eventually inherited much of the Templars' property.</note>, along with their estates. They also maintained themselves for a time in the regions of Luxembourg and Trier <margin>t)</margin>, until the bull of dissolution was gradually carried out everywhere, the announcement of which they were nowhere able to prevent.

As for the knights themselves, they were treated no more leniently at the Council of Vienne in France than they had been before. The pyres <note>original: "Scheiterhaufen"; refering to the stakes used for execution by burning.</note> that had been erected seven months prior were lit once again in various regions. Many were dragged from prison to their deaths; others took up secular clothing and spent their remaining sad days in the bosom of their families, in monasteries, or through manual labor. Some who considered themselves free and acquitted would have liked to marry, but the clergy <note>original: "Geistlichkeit"</note> opposed it; others fled to England, Cyprus, or Rhodes. Those who had been forced into confessions through torture <note>original: "Martern"</note> murmured both secretly and publicly about the barbarity and inhumanity of their judges.

One of these latter men, a Neapolitan, was brought before the Pope <note>Pope Clement V, who collaborated with King Philip IV to suppress the Order.</note> because of this; the Pope threatened him with the most painful death if he continued his complaints. All this could not frighten him; he answered boldly, calling the Pope an inhuman, unjust judge and leveling the most bitter reproaches against him. The enraged Pope had him placed in shackles and thrown into prison for a time, and since he persisted in his convictions, he condemned him to the fire for disobedience. The unfortunate man steadfastly watched the preparations for his death and summoned <note>original: "citirte"; a formal judicial summons, often used in a spiritual context to call someone to divine justice.</note> the Pope and King Philip to appear before God’s judgment <note>original: "Gottes Gericht"</note> within a year and a day, to give an account there of their conduct...
