# Jacques de Molay. #

[to appear and] give an account <note>original: "fahren abzulegen"; likely part of "Rechenschaft abzulegen," meaning to give an account of one's soul or actions before God.</note>. It is true that both the Pope and the King died within a year's time <note>Pope Clement V died in April 1314, and King Philip IV died in November 1314, both within months of the Grand Master's execution.</note> [w]. The historian who tells this relates it as nothing more than a mere rumor, as he was a contemporary of the Pope. He is also mistaken in stating that the number of Templars executed since 1308 was fifteen thousand; for there were scarcely that many in the Orient and the Occident <note>original: "Morgen- und Abendland"; the East (Crusader states) and the West (Europe).</note> combined. Furthermore, they were treated with much leniency in Spain, England, and Germany, and were for the most part executed only in France and Naples.

Around this time, their greatest adversary, Guillaume de Nogaret <note>The King’s advisor and mastermind behind the legal assault on the Templars.</note>, also died. It is said that he by chance encountered some knights who were being led to their deaths, and that they summoned him to appear before the judgment seat of God <note>original: "vor das Gericht Gottes geladen"; a formal spiritual summons to divine justice.</note> within eight days, and that he consequently died eight days later. Several writers, among them Meyer and the author of the *Chronicle of Asti*, recount his death in this manner; but Meyer is mistaken when he places his death in the year 1307; it is highly probable that Nogaret was still living in the year 1312 [x]. Everything seemed to promise the prisoners a favorable verdict; the compliance they had shown at Chinon <note>In 1308, at the Château de Chinon, the Pope’s representatives interrogated the Templar leaders. Nevertheless, the sentence declared that they should listen to the judgment of their condemnation publicly upon a scaffold, and then be sentenced to perpetual imprisonment. By means of the first point, the intention was to present these superiors publicly to the people as criminals, and to have them publicly declare that their Order was guilty of everything with which they had been charged until now. In this way, they sought to dispel any thought of their innocence, for many people, especially the Parisians, were indignant over the executions of so many men from the first families <note>The Knights Templar were largely drawn from the European nobility; "first families" refers to the high-ranking aristocratic houses of France.</note>.

<margin>a) Velly, *History of France*, regarding the year 1312.</margin>
...provided themselves for a judicial investigation, and for that reason set aside everything that could testify against them <margin>a</margin>.

This theory lacks substance. From 1305, the time when the malicious rumors about the Order first began, until August 1307, the knights could not have anticipated any judicial action; for not only was the plan of King Philip <note>King Philip IV of France, known as "the Fair," who orchestrated the downfall of the Templars to seize their wealth and cancel his debts.</note> still kept strictly secret, but the Pope <note>Pope Clement V.</note> overwhelmed the Grand Master with proofs of his confidence. At that time, the Pope was still writing to all princes and prelates to recommend the <term>Preceptor: a high-ranking official in the Templar Order who managed a province or a specific house</term> Blanke of Auvergne, who had placed himself at the head of a band of Crusaders. Furthermore, in a <term>Bulla: an official papal decree or public letter</term> dated August 2, 1307, the Pope still referred to the knights as his "dear sons" and the "brave soldiers of Christ." Even on the day before their arrest, the Grand Master in Paris received public marks of respect from the King. How, then, could they have suspected the gathering storm? From the coronation of the Pope until the time when the knights learned something of the plan against their Order, a year and a half had passed. The inquisitors, therefore, had ample time to seize some of these heads <note>Referring to the "idol heads" or Baphomet figures the Templars were accused of worshipping.</note> in order to convict the knights during interrogation. Philip’s end was no less sorrowful. The nobility and the clergy were embittered against him because of new taxes; he found himself in the dilemma of either waging war against his own realm or retracting everything. The wives of his three sons were publicly accused of adultery, and two of them were convicted of this crime; the shame that this brought upon his family, along with various secret sorrows, brought on an illness against which the physicians wasted their skills in vain. He died at Fontainebleau on November 9th, and of the four sons he had, the youngest died as a child, while the other three ascended the throne one after another; within fourteen years, no male descendant of his could be found <note>This refers to the end of the direct Capetian dynasty, as all of Philip's sons died without male heirs, leading to the rise of the House of Valois and the Hundred Years' War.</note>. In England, the pensions for the remaining Templars were paid so poorly that some fell into the greatest destitution and were in danger of starving; consequently, the Archbishop of Canterbury <note>Walter Reynolds, who held the office from 1313–1327.</note> felt compelled to make representations against this to the Grand Master of the Hospitallers <margin>f)</margin>. The Hospitallers, however, had by no means received all the estates of the English Templars; many of these remained in foreign hands. The argument was made that Parliament had not authorized their transfer and that, according to the laws of the land, they belonged neither to the Pope nor to the Hospitallers, but to the Crown.

In Germany and other regions, these estates fell to the local sovereigns and were partly scattered, sold, exchanged, or otherwise alienated. # A p p e n d i x.

It is undeniable that the Pope <note>Pope Clement V (reigned 1305–1314), who issued the bull *Vox in excelso* to suppress the Order.</note>, King Philip <note>Philip IV of France, known as "the Fair," who was the primary driver behind the trials and dissolution of the Templars.</note>, and the Hospitallers <note>The Order of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, who were the legal heirs to most Templar properties.</note> drew the greatest advantage from the suppression of the Templars. One could cite entire lists of estates and possessions that fell to the former two because of it. Regarding the Hospitallers, it is known that since the union of the Templar estates with their Order, most of their knights possessed Commanderies <term>Commandery: An estate or manor under the control of a Commander within a military order.</term>. These riches were hardly beneficial to the observance of the Order's rule; the Commanders rarely came to Rhodes <note>The Mediterranean island of Rhodes served as the sovereign headquarters of the Hospitallers from 1310 until 1522.</note>; they gradually withdrew from obedience to their superiors, and instead of the novices and knights whom each Commander was supposed to maintain in his house, one saw only a multitude of servants, pages, and hunters. Even the relatives of these Commanders faithfully helped consume the income that was actually intended for the support of the poor and the defense of the Christian states. The alms, which the Templars had distributed regularly and abundantly, fell into oblivion; the Commanders thought only of their pleasure, every undertaking was neglected, and even the pilgrims were without protection. Everyone murmured about it, and it was suggested to the Pope that the Templar estates be taken away from the Hospitallers again, and

# Appendix.
Tempelherrnord. 2. B. S <note>Abbreviation for "History of the Order of the Templars, Vol 2, Page [Signature mark]"</note>

Finally, as for the fairness or unfairness of the extermination <note>original: "Ausrottung"</note> of the order, one cannot deny that an order which, like this one, performed such important services for religion, deserved some respect; furthermore, a society that submits to the laws of the state must be tolerated, because one is duty-bound to tolerate everything that does not run contrary to the common good. To discover, however, whether the Templars <term>Templars: Also known as the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon, a Catholic military order founded in 1119.</term> were in this latter category or not, one should not rely on the testimonies of their enemies. Instead, one should have questioned the poor whom they supported on their estates and in the field, the sick they cared for in the hospitals, and the prisoners they ransomed from the Saracens <term>Saracens: A medieval term used by Europeans to refer to Muslims, particularly during the Crusades.</term>. Furthermore, after the loss of Palestine, the order had become anything but superfluous. In Spain, there were still borders to protect, cities to defend, and armies of Moors <term>Moors: Muslim inhabitants of the Maghreb, the Iberian Peninsula, Sicily, and Malta during the Middle Ages.</term> to fight; for this reason, the kings of Portugal and Aragon found themselves forced, immediately after the suppression of the Templars, to found new knightly orders with the same purpose and intent, and a few years later, the King of Armenia had to call upon the Hospitallers <term>Hospitallers: The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, a military order similar to the Templars that focused on medical care and defense of the Holy Land.</term> for help.

# Appendix.

Finally, as for the corruption attributed to the Order, one of our most insightful writers expresses himself in the following manner: “It is not believable that religious knights, who are bound to the Gospel by their duty and to their fatherland by the bonds of blood, should suddenly renounce all sense of religion, virtue, and humanity. Private individuals can hide their character during their lifetime, but whole societies—famous societies that were so often attacked and defended—can be accurately judged after the passage of two centuries. It would be unjust to wish to condemn them based on unfavorable rumors, uncertain conjectures, and unfounded suspicion.”

Before the year 1305, the Order of the Temple <term>Order of the Temple: The Knights Templar.</term> stood in the same high regard as the Order of the Hospitallers <term>Hospitallers: The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, a contemporary military order that focused on medical care as well as defense.</term>, and the shameful idiom, *to drink like a Templar* <note>original: "trinken wie ein Tempelherr"</note>, had not yet been invented at that time. This expression was the invention of some idle mind, and entirely worthy of Rabelais <note>François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553), a French Renaissance writer known for his bawdy humor and satire.</note>, who first used it in his *Gargantua* <note>A famous satirical novel by Rabelais titled "The Very Horrific Life of the Great Gargantua."</note>. Baluzius <note>Étienne Baluze (1630–1718), a French scholar and librarian who compiled vast collections of medieval documents.</note>, who carefully sought out everything concerning the customs of that era, found tha<unclear>...</unclear>

# Appendix.

people also used to say *to drink like a Pope* <note>original Latin: *bibere Papaliter*</note>, but before the eradication of the Order of the Temple, one finds in no writer that anyone said *to drink like a Templar* <note>original Latin: *bibere Templariter*</note>. But assuming that this latter phrase became a proverb among the common people, perhaps the following gave occasion for it: The Rule of the Order <note>The Latin Rule of the Templars, established at the Council of Troyes in 1129, governed every aspect of the knights' lives, from their clothing to their conduct in battle</note> prescribed that when the Templars ate in the refectory <note>a communal dining hall in a monastery or religious house</note>, they sat two by two at a table, and these two had to be served as much food as would suffice to satisfy four of them. The reason for this abundance at the table was so that the poor, who always received the leftovers from the refectory, might also be provided for. This custom, which arose from a feeling of compassion, was later used to bring the Order into ill repute.

In general, one could have reformed the Order without destroying it completely, if other people had not been so intent on its total downfall. "Suppose," says the Friend of Humanity <note>original German: *Menschenfreund*; likely a reference to an Enlightenment philosopher or a specific author advocating for social justice</note>, "that the soldier class were without discipline, the authorities without conscience, and the nobility without a sense of virtue—should one therefore [eradi-] <meta>catchword: auss- (German: ausrotten)</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the origins of common proverbs regarding Templar drinking and explains how their charitable practice of over-serving food for the benefit of the poor was later used to smear the Order's reputation. It concludes with an argument from 'the Friend of Humanity' suggesting that corruption in an institution should lead to reform rather than total destruction.</summary>
<keywords>bibere Papaliter, bibere Templariter, Templar Rule, refectory, charity, Knight Templar reputation, social reform, philanthropy</keywords>

# Appendix.

...cate? <note>The catchword from the previous page was *auss-* to complete the German word *ausrotten*, meaning "to eradicate" or "to root out."</note> The principle of suppression and destruction contradicts every reasonable form of government and is equivalent to the generosity of suicide. An ignorant surgeon <term>surgeon<gloss>original German: *Wundarzt*; literally a "wound-doctor," these were historical medical practitioners who performed external surgeries and amputations, often distinguished from university-educated physicians</gloss></term> cuts off a leg that a wise physician would have carefully treated and preserved; if one assumes four treatments in the manner of the former, nothing remains but the torso i).
